activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
Peyton arrived at the health office fifteen minutes early, her notes folded into quarters inside her jacket pocket, because the peer educator training had one rule she kept repeating to herself: know it well enough that you don't read it off the page. Ms. Schneider had assigned each trainee a topic and a practice audience, and Peyton had drawn consent, contraception, and testing, the whole trifecta, which Kristen had called "the heavy package" and Kaeden had called "a landing you'll stick, probably."

The practice audience was real, not hypothetical. Kaeden sat on the counter of the empty chemistry lab with his ankles crossed, and Kristen pulled a stool over and said, before Peyton had even finished unfolding her notes, "Okay, but say someone actually wants to get tested. Doesn't a parent have to sign something? Like for anything medical when you're under eighteen?"

Peyton's mouth opened and nothing came out. She had rehearsed consent until she could say it plainly: that it has to be freely given, that you can change your mind at any point, that being silent isn't the same as saying yes. She had the contraception part down too, the different methods and how effectiveness actually works, which Kaeden had argued about for ten minutes last week until he conceded, slowly, like a man recuperating from a defeat he still half believed he hadn't lost. But the testing question, the practical machinery of it, she had skipped it, assuming it would sort itself out.

"I don't actually know," she said, and Kristen's face did the thing faces do when they'd hoped for an answer. "I'll find out. Give me until tomorrow."

That afternoon she walked to the clinic two blocks past the bagel shop, because a fact you look up alone in your bedroom felt different from a fact you stood inside of. The waiting room smelled like disinfectus and old magazines. The nurse at the desk was filling out a form and didn't look up until Peyton said, "I have a question, not an appointment."

"Those are my favorite kind," the nurse said.

"Say a seventeen-year-old wants to get tested for infections. Does a parent have to sign a form?"

The nurse set down her pen. "No. All fifty states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission. Some states do set a minimum age, so it's worth checking yours." She said it in the flat, tired, certain tone of someone who had said it many times and would say it many more, and then she slid a pamphlet across the desk, the way you'd hand someone an umbrella.

Peyton walked home turning it over. She had spent the week building arguments for her presentation, and she'd been proud of the structure of it, the clean logic she'd privately thought of as its logos, the way each point earned the next. But standing at the clinic she understood that the reasoning wasn't the load-bearing part. Kristen didn't need persuasion; she needed a door and confirmation that it was unlocked. A presentation that proved people ought to have access, when the access already existed, would be tautological, an argument for a thing already granted, and worse than useless, because it would leave Kristen standing outside with her question unanswered.

The next day Peyton stood in front of the same lab counter, same audience, same notes she now barely looked at. She explained consent first, slowly, letting the silence after "you can change your mind at any point" actually sit there. She walked them through the methods, and Kaeden interrupted to ask a question he would never have asked a month ago, which she counted as a kind of change, though not one she named out loud. Then Kristen raised her hand, formally, as if they were still in a classroom and not an empty lab after last bell.

"Did you find out? About the form?"

"No form," Peyton said. "All fifty states and Washington, DC let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission. Some states set a minimum age, so you'd want to check ours." She spread the pamphlet flat on the counter between them, and Kristen pulled it closer, not picking it up yet, just resting two fingers on it like it might still be taken back.

"Wait," Kaeden said. "So the whole time I've been telling guys it's basically impossible until you're eighteen, I've been, what, making that up?"

"You've been repeating something you never checked," Peyton said.

Kristen folded the pamphlet into her back pocket, and Peyton watched her do it, the small ordinary motion of it, and thought about how little of the week's careful structure had actually mattered, and how much this single folded piece of paper might.

"You want me to go with you?" Kaeden asked Kristen, and it came out gruff, his ears going pink. "Saturday, I mean. Not for anything. Just the walking part."

Kristen looked at him for a long second. "Yeah," she said. "The walking part."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: The word 'mortgage' comes from Old French for 'dead pledge', because the pledge ends either when the debt is paid or when the property is forfeited.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold air, and Chloe sat in one of the gray chairs by the mortgage desk while her mother arranged and rearranged the folder of papers in her lap. On the desk between them sat a calculator, a brochure with a smiling couple on the cover, and a small fish tank whose water had gone turbid over the yellow gravel, so the fish appeared and vanished like thoughts she couldn't finish. Chloe's mother had said only two things on the drive over: that the rent on their apartment was going up in June, and that maybe it was time to stop paying someone else's mortgage and start paying their own.

"Ms. Kovalenko will walk us through it," her mother said now, low, as though the other waiting customers might grade them. "Don't say anything about the late payment last fall."

"You told me to be honest."

"I told you not to volunteer."

Ms. Kovalenko came out from behind the glass with a lanyard swinging and a stack of forms. She was younger than Chloe had expected, maybe thirty, and she shook Chloe's hand too, which nobody ever did. "You're the financial acumen in the family, I hear," she said. "Your mom says you do the budget on the fridge whiteboard."

"Sort of," Chloe said, though she felt the word land somewhere warmer than it deserved.

The numbers came out one at a time. Ms. Kovalenko talked about deposits, how the money in their savings account showed the bank they could actually set cash aside, and about the down payment, the chunk of the house's price paid up front so the loan would be smaller. Fifteen thousand was what they had. The apartment they'd looked at in Fairview was listed at one hundred ninety. Chloe did the division in her head and didn't like the answer, so she did it again on the calculator while her mother explained the late payment before being asked, preempting the question Ms. Kovalenko hadn't gotten around to yet, which made her cheeks go pink but kept her voice steady.

"There's a program for first-time buyers," Ms. Kovalenko said. "Smaller down payment, mortgage insurance on top. It's not free money. It's a longer road."

"How long?" Chloe asked.

"For people in your position? Sometimes ten years before it stops feeling like drowning. Sometimes five."

Chloe's phone buzzed. Mae, from the row of chairs by the window, where she'd been waiting for an hour because Chloe had promised her a ride to the mall afterward and Mae had decided to come inside rather than sit in the hot car: did u know the fish tank is gross. Chloe typed back that she'd noticed. Then Mae appeared beside the desk, chin over Chloe's shoulder, utterly without shame.

"Is this a mortgage?" Mae asked. "My parents fight about theirs at Thanksgiving."

"It's a meeting about maybe getting one," Chloe's mother said.

Mae squinted at the form. "Weird word, mortgage. Why is it called that? It sounds like a sea monster."

Chloe had looked this up two weeks ago, the night after her grandfather had leaned across his kitchen table, tapped his coffee mug, and asked her the same question, testing her like he always did. She said, "It comes from Old French. It means dead pledge."

"Dead?" Mae stepped back a little. "Dead how?"

"The pledge dies either way," Chloe said. "Either you pay it off and it's finished, or the property's forfeited and the debt dies with it. Either way, the pledge ends." Her grandfather had liked that answer, had said it was the most honest word in finance, a word that admitted up front what both exits looked like.

Ms. Kovalenko had stopped writing. "That's actually right," she said. "Most people never ask."

"It doesn't scare you?" Mae said to Chloe's mother. "A word like that?"

Chloe's mother looked at the folder, at the fish tank, at the calculator with its ugly division still glowing. "Renting scares me more," she said. "Rent goes up and you pay it forever and own nothing at the end. At least a dead pledge dies eventually."

"Or it takes the house with it," Chloe said, because somebody in the room had to hold that side of it, and her mother could not, today, afford to.

"Or it does," Ms. Kovalenko said. "Which is why I'm not going to approve anything today. I'm going to give you a worksheet, and a number to reach for the deposit side, and we'll look again in the spring." She slid a page across the desk with a column of blank lines, like a form for a person who didn't quite exist yet but might.

In the car afterward, Mae fiddled with the radio and said the whole thing had sounded like drowning with extra steps. Chloe said maybe, but the fridge whiteboard was hers, and fifteen thousand was already real, sitting in an account with both their names on it, earning something small every month while they slept. The spring was eight months away. She turned onto the boulevard and, at the long red light by the pawnshop, took out her phone and made a new column heading under the grocery list.

"First deposit," she said out loud, typing it. Mae read it over her shoulder and said, "That's the little one, right, not the down payment?"

"That's the little one."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Selected Works section asks for 5 artworks and counts for 40 percent of the score.
story:
Abigail counted the paintings twice, because the first count had to be wrong. Five for the Selected Works section, forty percent of the score, and the other half of the portfolio riding on the sustained investigation, which she had not started. She stood in the gallery with her phone in her hand, the deadline forty-one days away, and told herself she was here for research.

She was here because Ms. Halvorsen had said her last ten pieces looked like ten different artists had made them. Abigail disagreed with that. She thought the pieces were versatile, which was a word she had used out loud in class and which Harmony had repeated back to her in a voice that made it clear the word had not survived the exchange.

The gallery was showing a retrospective of a printmaker who had spent thirty years on harbor lights. Same subject, different weather. Abigail walked the perimeter with her sketchbook and did not write anything down. The work was an encapsulation of one obsession, she thought, and the thought felt like something she had read on a wall label rather than something she knew. She read the wall label anyway. It said the artist had chosen the harbor because it was the view from her childhood window, and Abigail felt a small unfairness, that some people were handed their theme at birth.

Eliza was already in the back room, sitting on the bench with her portfolio binder open across her knees. "You're staring at the wall," Eliza said.

"I'm synthesizing."

"You're stalling." Eliza turned a page. She had eleven finished pieces and was cutting down to five, and she was doing it by laying the weakest ones face down, one at a time, without hesitating. Abigail watched her flip the fourth one, a charcoal self-portrait that Abigail personally thought was the best thing in the binder.

"Why that one?"

"It's off-theme. I love it and it doesn't belong." Eliza closed the binder. "Forty percent is Selected Works. Five pieces. I'm not wasting a slot on something that doesn't argue for the investigation."

Abigail had known the numbers, had written them on a sticky note above her desk at home, but she had been treating the five as a separate problem from the ten, when they were the same problem. She had been choosing her best work instead of choosing work that said one thing. She sat down on the bench.

"I have nine pieces and no theme," she said.

"What are the nine of?"

"They're of whatever I felt like."

"That's not a theme, that's a mood board." Eliza said it without cruelty, the way she said most things. "What do you look at?"

Abigail started to say she looked at everything, and then did not, because it wasn't true. She opened her sketchbook to the pages she never showed anyone, the ones she did at the kitchen table after her mother's shift ended. Windows. The window over the sink, the windows of the building across the alley, the window of the laundromat at night. She had never thought of them as a subject because they were just where her eyes went.

Eliza looked through the pages without touching them. "There's your ten."

Abigail said the window pieces weren't finished, weren't good, and Eliza said that was a different problem than having no theme, and a solvable one. Abigail pointed out, reasonably, that being bad was worse than being off-theme. Eliza shrugged. "Bad you can fix. Random you can't."

They walked out through the front room together, past the harbor lights, and Abigail stopped at the last print, a night one, fog so thick the light was just a smear. She had walked past it the first time. Now it looked like the view from her mother's kitchen window in November, and she took out her phone and photographed it, then wrote in her sketchbook: glass, not the thing behind it. She did not know yet if that was the theme or only a sentence, and she was honest with herself about that much.

In the parking lot Harmony was leaning against Eliza's car waiting for a ride, and asked what the gallery had been like. Abigail said there was a printmaker who had painted the same harbor for thirty years. Harmony asked if that wasn't boring, and Abigail heard herself say that she used to think so. She had her keys in her hand and the sketchbook under her arm, and she told them she was going home to look at the window over the sink. Then she got in her car and sat there a moment before starting it, thinking about the smeared light through the fog.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
Xavier's grandmother had a system for the diyas that she refused to write down. Cotton wicks first, then oil to the rim, then a wet finger around each clay lip so the flame wouldn't catch the edge. She demonstrated on the first one and handed him the box of two hundred, which meant he was doing the rest. Her back porch smelled of cardamom from the kitchen and kerosene from the lamps, and by four o'clock the whole courtyard wall had a soft orange spine running along it, one flame every handspan.

His grandmother went inside to argue with the pressure cooker, and Xavier kept working. He had done this since he was nine, but this year he had started actually thinking about it, mostly because of an argument with Angel in the parking lot on Tuesday. Angel had called religion a system for people who couldn't handle uncertainty, and Xavier had said something about light and darkness that sounded, even at the time, like a fortune cookie. He wanted a better version. He just didn't have one yet.

The doorbell rang at five, which was early. Lacey stood on the mat holding a foil tray of something her mother had made, blinking at the porch. "Are those candles? Like, a hundred candles?"

"Oil lamps," Xavier said. "They're called diyas." He set down the wick he was twisting. "You put them in rows everywhere, the house and the temple too, doesn't matter. It's Diwali."

"Is that, like, Hindu Christmas?"

"Kind of, except Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, some Buddhists all do it. It's not just one thing." He heard his grandmother's voice in that sentence, and he also heard himself saying it as though he had known it his whole life, when in fact he had learned it in February from a museum placard while on a school trip he'd mostly spent trying to see if Lacey was looking at him.

She followed him along the wall while he worked. "So what's the point? Of the lamps specifically."

"The light wins," Xavier said. "Darkness is the thing, and you put out light, and the light wins." Saying it out loud, it sounded less like a fortune cookie and more like an instruction, something you did with your hands.

Inside, the argument with the pressure cooker had expanded into an argument with the pressure cooker and Mrs. Mehta from two doors down, who had come over to drop off mathri and stayed to supervise. Xavier's grandmother was Hindu. Mrs. Mehta was Jain, and the two of them disagreed about everything except the lamp oil, which Mrs. Mehta had opinions about the way other women had opinions about grandchildren. In the kitchen doorway stood the Manns' son from across the street, sixteen and Sikh, who had come to return a tarp and been captured by the snack table. Xavier watched them for a minute through the screen: three traditions in one kitchen, all of them shouting cheerfully about the same festival, all of them right.

Angel texted at seven, while Xavier was re-lighting the ones the wind had killed: still think it's all a grift? And Xavier stood there with a wet finger and a match and genuinely did not know. The lamps worked whether or not you believed anything, the way a lighthouse worked. The light literally overcame the darkness; that part was not a metaphor, it was measurable. And yet his grandmother sang while she cooked, and Mrs. Mehta had come in her good sari, and if it was a grift, it was the least efficient one ever run, run by volunteers who did all their own dishes. Angel would say the comfort didn't make it true. His grandmother would say true wasn't the only category that mattered. Xavier could interpolate between those two positions all night, but somewhere between the second matchbox and the third, he noticed he was smiling, which was data neither position accounted for.

A diya near the gate guttered out. He knelt on the cold bricks and relit it, cupping the flame, and behind him the front door opened and Lacey came out with two paper cups of something sweet. She sat down on the step beside him without asking and held one out. "So is this the part where you tell me what you figured out?"

"Still working on it," he said, and took the cup.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon was a prison design with a central tower from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were.
story:
Sophie discovered the letter at 4:40 on a Tuesday, folded into her inbox between a college mailing and a sale notice from a store she never shopped at. The district, it said, had adopted a new student safety platform. All school-issued accounts would be monitored for "indicators of concern," and parents would be notified of any flagged activity. She read it twice, then opened a new tab and typed the name of the software, because the letter described what it did but not how, and the gap between those two things bothered her the way a loose thread bothers a sleeve.

The company's website was cheerful, all soft blues and stock photos of smiling teenagers. Its algorithm, the page claimed, could detect incipient self-harm, violence, and bullying before adults noticed anything. There was a section for parents, a section for administrators, and no section for students, which Sophie found telling. She scrolled until she reached a paragraph about how the system had been "trained on millions of student interactions," and she copied the phrase into her notes without knowing yet what she would do with it.

What drove her, if she was honest, was Bailey. Two weeks earlier, Bailey had been called out of sixth period, and had come back quiet and then, days later, furious: a counselor had met her with printouts of her searches, all of them for an English essay on Hamlet and suicide, the assignment Ms. Clarke-Williams herself had set. What stung Bailey most was not the meeting but the printouts, the fact that someone, somewhere, had been reading along the whole time. Emma-Rose had done the same searches on her phone, at home, on the family network, and no one had ever called her out of class. Sophie had spent enough time on her own laptop to know that fairness was not the default setting of anything, and she wanted to know why the system saw some students and not others.

At the kitchen table, her mother asked what the letter meant, and Sophie said probably nothing, probably it catches kids who actually need catching. She said it lightly. Then she went upstairs, opened her laptop, and searched "who watches the watchers," which felt melodramatic until she found Bentham.

Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon, her screen told her, was a prison design with a central tower from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were. She sat with that for a while. The prisoners' uncertainty was the mechanism and the punishment at once; the tower barely needed anyone in it. She thought of the little green dot on her school account, of how she had started typing differently since Tuesday, deleting phrases, softening searches, conducting a small private audit of every sentence as though a stranger were grading her sincerity. It sensitized her to her own behavior in a way that felt almost useful, almost like a skill, and she hated that it worked.

At school the next morning she asked Ms. Clarke-Williams whether they could talk about the monitoring for the Hamlet unit, surveillance and Denmark, watchers who are watched. Ms. Clarke-Williams said, "You mean the panopticon, like the prison tower," and approved the angle but added, quietly, that she had not been consulted about the software and had no visibility into its flags. That was the first crack in Sophie's assumption that some adult was in the tower. She filed a records request through the student portal, using language she had copied from a legal aid website, asking which students had been flagged and on what basis.

The response arrived Friday, redacted, and it was the twist she had not predicted. The flags were not apportioned by behavior at all, or not only. Students on school-issued devices were flagged; students on personal devices were not. Students from families that had checked a box on the free-lunch form, which enrolled them in a district program that issued laptops, were the ones being read. Bailey had a district laptop because her family had checked that box. Emma-Rose had her own phone because she could. The algorithm wasn't biased in some mysterious way; it was biased the way a doorway with a step is biased, plainly, structurally, to anyone willing to measure.

Sophie printed the redacted pages, highlighted the pattern in yellow, and carried them to Bailey's locker before first period. She had a considered sentence ready, something about how the watching was real but unevenly aimed, and how she still didn't know whether the right answer was less watching or fairer watching, since the flags had once caught a boy at another school who had needed catching. Bailey took the pages and read them against the locker door, and the hallway noise filled the space where a lesson might have gone. "So they built the tower," Bailey said slowly, "and only gave some of us cells." Sophie nodded, and reached over to fold the top page back so the highlighted lines showed, side by side.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
The keys were heavier than Jake expected, and colder, as if the car had been holding them somewhere out of the sun. His mother had left the sedan in the driveway with the tank full and a note under the wiper that said, Be better than I was at this. He was still reading it when Ms. Xu came down the walk from next door, carrying a battered clipboard and a thermos, wearing the same grey cardigan she wore when she watered her roses at six in the morning.

"You'll want your phone off," she said, opening the passenger door. "Not silent. Off."

He turned it off, and only then remembered the text he hadn't answered, the one Christina had sent an hour ago: Lesson was a disaster. Forgot my belt, still in the driveway, and she just sat there. Five minutes. FIVE. He should have asked what she meant, but there had been no time, because Ms. Xu was already buckling her own belt with a click that sounded final, like a door being locked from the inside.

"Mirror first," she said. "Then seat. Then we talk."

He adjusted the mirror until the driveway fence filled the glass, then the street, then a sliver of Ms. Xu's cardigan. He moved the seat forward. His foot found the brake. The engine started with a shudder that traveled up through his spine, and he gripped the wheel at ten and two the way the pamphlet had shown, the pamphlet he had read four times last night in bed, mostly to avoid reading the financial aid forms beside it. Somewhere in that pamphlet had been a statistic, printed in a box, and he tried to pull it up out of memory while Ms. Xu watched the street.

"Your friend was here Tuesday," Ms. Xu said. "Christina. Bright girl. She got in the car and reached for the ignition before she reached for anything else. So we sat in the driveway for five minutes, and she cried a little, and then she put on her belt and we had a very good lesson. Do you think I was cruel?"

"I think she still isn't over it," Jake said. "She texted me in all caps."

"Good. Then it amortized over the whole hour." Ms. Xu unscrewed the thermos and did not drink. "Every minute of a lesson costs the same. A wasted minute in the driveway costs no more than a wasted minute on Route 9. But a habit costs less the earlier you pay it."

"That's not really how the word works," Jake said, and immediately wished he hadn't, because she turned to look at him fully for the first time.

"No," she said. "It isn't. But you understood me."

He had. That was the strange part. His father used words like that to sound impressive, dropping them at dinner parties like coins on a table, and Jake had privately decided years ago that anyone who talked that way was probably a charlatan. But Ms. Xu wasn't performing; she was just an old woman who liked precision and had read one too many articles about compound interest, maybe, or none at all. He filed the distinction somewhere and let it go.

"Christina thinks you're unreasonable," he said. "She said the driveway isn't even a road."

"The driveway is where the habit starts." Ms. Xu set the thermos in the cup holder without drinking. "Tell me why it matters. Not that it matters. Why."

He looked at the fence in the mirror, then at his hands. The pamphlet box surfaced slowly, the way things did when he didn't force them. "The CDC," he said. "Wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half." He heard his own voice say it, flat and strange, like a sentence that belonged to someone else, someone who had done the reading. "Half. Not a little. Half."

"And Christina thinks five minutes in a driveway is unreasonable," Ms. Xu said.

The street was empty and interminable in both directions, the new asphalt pale in the afternoon light. He eased off the brake and the car rolled, and he turned the wheel too hard, corrected, corrected again, and Ms. Xu said nothing at all, which was somehow louder than Christina's all-caps text. They went around the block. Twice. On the third pass he signaled before the corner without being told, and she made a small sound, approving, almost inaudible.

It was on the fourth pass, slowing for the stop sign at the end of his own street, that she said, "My sister didn't wear one. Same age you are now." She said it to the windshield, not to him. "So when a student reaches for the ignition first, I sit."

Jake stopped the car at the sign, fully, wheels motionless, and looked over. Ms. Xu was still looking at the windshield. He wanted to say something about the statistic, about half, about how numbers were supposed to make things smaller and instead made this one enormous, but none of it came out right in his head, so he said nothing either.

"Turn left here," Ms. Xu said. "And check your mirror first."

He checked the mirror. The fence slid away behind them, and the street opened up.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key, so a movement in C major moves to G major.
story:
The church hall smelled of candle wax and old hymnals, and Avery spread the photocopied score across the piano bench before the last of the evening service crowd had cleared the vestibule. Mozart, Sonata in C, K. 545, first movement. She had until Monday to mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation with coloured pencil, and she had promised Ms. Bui she would mark by ear, not just by eye, which was why she had begged the use of the church piano on a Sunday night.

The problem was that Avery did not trust her ear. She had played flute for six years and piano for three, and she could follow a melody well enough, but the moment a second tune arrived, slippery and cheerful, she could not say for certain whether the music had truly changed key or merely wandered somewhere colourful and come home again. Ms. Bui, the church organist, had been blunt about it. "If you cannot hear where the second theme begins," she had said, arranging the copies on the desk, "you will mark the wrong bar and your whole analysis collapses." Ms. Biu had a reputation as irascible, and the rumour was that she had once made a chorister cry over a held breath in the wrong place, so Avery had not argued.

Her phone buzzed against the music rack. A message from Kayley, sent from the library across town: "I found a recording but it's the whole sonata, 15 min, no track marks. Kelly-Anne says her brother did this movement last year and got the second theme wrong and Ms. Bui wrote 'you impugn the entire exposition' on his sheet. Not joking. She actually wrote that." Avery read it twice, then typed back: "What did he get wrong??" Kayley's reply came slowly, as though she were being careful. "He marked the second theme in bar 10. It's later. That's all Kelly-Anne remembers."

Avery set the phone face down. Bars one through four, she could hear already, were the first theme, simple and bright, the kind of tune that announced itself the way a beginner announced a C major scale. What she could not yet tell was when the exposition left that theme behind, and whether the second theme was the passage with the trills or the one after it. She put her hands on the keys, then took them off, then put them on again, because Ms. Bui had also said, more gently, "Play it badly if you must, but play it whole."

She played the opening. Her fingering was clumsy on the runs and she clipped the ends of phrases, but the shape came through. Somewhere past the first page a new tune arrived, lighter, more singing, and something about it felt different in a way she could not name, the way a room felt different when a window opened in it. She stopped. She bent over the score and looked, not at the notes, but at the little cluster of sharps beside the treble clef where the new tune began. One sharp. She counted it three times. One sharp meant F was raised, and F raised meant G major. She sat back, hearing the tune again in her memory, testing it, and found she could hear it now, the pull upward, the whole second theme sitting in G. She wrote in the margin, in pencil, "second theme, G major," and underneath, smaller, "exposition moves from C major to G major."

The door at the back of the hall clicked open. Ms. Bui came down the aisle carrying a thermos, and Avery's hand went flat over her pencil marks as though to hide them. Ms. Bui did not look at her. She sat in the second pew from the front, unscrewed the thermos, and said, "Continue. You stopped in the middle of a thought."

"I found where the second theme starts," Avery said. Her voice sounded younger than she wanted it to. "In G major."

Ms. Bui drank, watching her. "And why does that matter to you? Kelly-Anne's brother, last year, told me it didn't. He said the key was decoration." There was a silence in which Avery understood that this was the actual test, and that everything before it had only been preparation. She thought about the window feeling, the tune pulling upward, the way Mozart had wanted the second idea to stand apart from the first rather than repeat it in lighter clothing. She also thought, honestly, that she could not yet explain why a composer would choose the dominant rather than some other key, and that her certainty about the shift itself might be luck.

"It matters because it's how the exposition is built," she said slowly. "The first theme is in C, the second theme is in G, and the whole first part of the movement depends on that move. But I don't know yet how the development uses it. I haven't marked that far." Ms. Bui set the thermos down on the pew beside her, and the pew creaked, and she did not smile exactly, but something around her eyes loosened.

"Then you have until Monday," Ms. Bui said. "Play me to the end of the exposition, and when the second theme comes, do not slow down to admire it. Let it arrive." Avery put her hands back on the keys, found C major under her fingers, and began.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love.
story:
Makayla stood close enough to the painting to see the hairline cracks in its surface, which was closer than Ms. Hamdan had told them to stand, and she did not step back. The assignment sheet in her pocket said formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism, no biography, no feelings about the artist's life. She had already crossed out two opening sentences in her notebook, one of which began "Frida Kahlo suffered greatly," because Ms. Hamdan had read that sentence aloud to the whole class last week and asked, pleasantly, what colour the suffering was.

The gallery had hung Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird on a wall of its own, and the room was cold in the way museums are cold, the air dry and faintly chemical. Behind Makayla, Trace angled his phone at the canvas and then lowered it, disappointed. The gallery forbade photographs, and besides, he wanted a picture of himself in front of it, not the painting itself, something for the account he was building before orientation started in the fall. "One of you two has to take it when the guard walks away," he said. Carmen said she was not getting thrown out of a museum three weeks before she had to write a college essay about a time she showed integrity.

Carmen had her own notebook out, filled already, because Carmen prepared for everything. "The background's dark green, tropical, but it's flattened, like fabric behind her," she said. "And the animals are placed in a vertical line. Cat on her shoulder, monkey, then the bird at her throat. That's composition, that's a whole paragraph." Makayla wrote it down, then stopped. She had been staring at the hummingbird for nearly ten minutes, its small body hanging upside down from the thorn necklace, wings folded, and she could not make it fit. The monkey tugged the thorns like a child picking at a scab. The black cat watched with its flat green eyes. But the bird was dead, and it hung at her throat like a pendant, like something chosen.

Her instinct, the instinct Ms. Hamdan kept pushing against, was to say the bird was a symbol of death, of pain worn openly, and then to mention the bus accident, the surgeries, the years spent lying in bed to convalesce while she painted herself because she was the subject always available. Makayla could write that paper in her sleep. She had written it, more or less, in tenth grade. The problem was that it explained everything and noticed nothing, and standing here she could see it was not even accurate, because a pendant is not a wound. A pendant is put on. It is worn the way you wear a thing you want.

A grandmother came through with a boy of maybe seven, the boy tugging toward the exit and the grandmother pausing, as people did, in front of the small famous face. The boy pointed at the hummingbird and asked why the bird was dead. "It's a charm," his grandmother said. "For luck in love." Then she took his hand and they moved on toward the café, and Makayla stood very still, as if the sentence were an insect that might fly away if she breathed.

A dead bird for luck in love. She turned it over the way she had learned to turn over a line of poetry, testing it against the thorns, which drew a thin line of blood at the artist's neck, against the dragonflies stacked symmetrically on either side of her, against the expression, which was not grieving. It was even. It was almost pleasant, the face of someone considering something. So the painting was not a display of suffering, Makayla thought, or not only that; it was a display of contradiction, sorrow arranged as ornament, hope hung up dead and still hoped in. She did not know if that was a thesis or just a fancier way of saying she liked it. She wrote it down anyway, in the margin, where she kept the things she was not sure of.

Trace had found the guard at the far end of the room and stationed Carmen by the fire exit, and he was grinning, phone raised, motioning for Makayla to come stand beside the painting and act natural. She went, because he was her friend and because the guard was already turning back around, and Carmen hissed at them both from the doorway. In the photograph, if it survived, Makayla would be slightly blurred, caught mid-step, looking not at the camera but back over her shoulder at the green wall and the small woman with the bleeding neck and the dead bird she wore for luck. "Got it," Trace whispered, and the phone vanished into his jacket.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
The bowling alley smelled of rented shoes and floor wax, and Evan stood at the counter trying to remember whether size ten was the size he actually wore or the size he had claimed the last time he was here. The girl behind the counter, whose name tag said nothing he could read without staring, waited with the patience of someone who had inured herself to teenagers a long time ago. Behind him, Chad kept clearing his throat.

"You're holding up cosmic bowling," Chad said. "Lanes go dark at nine. It's eight fifteen."

"My date is at the snack bar," Evan said. "Her name is Dia. Be normal."

"I'm always normal. You're the one who practiced a handshake in the parking lot."

Evan took his shoes and the shoes he had ordered for Dia, size eight, a guess he had made from the gym class seating chart, and this guess now struck him as the kind of detail a person could be wrong about in a way that mattered. In Mr. Bouchard's class last spring they had spent a full period on surveys and statistics instead of the scheduled unit on the Gilded Age, and Evan, who had been avoiding an essay, had read the whole handout. One line had stuck: in the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. He had copied it into his notebook because it seemed like the sort of thing a person should keep, though he had not known yet what he would do with it.

Dia waved from the snack bar, pretzel in hand, and Evan's stomach performed a maneuver he chose not to analyze. But before he reached her, he saw Jaylen two lanes over with his girlfriend, the one from the choir concert, the one Jaylen had been seeing for six weeks and described only in adjectives like intense and committed. As Evan watched, she reached over and grabbed Jaylen's forearm to pull him back from the lane, and Jaylen's whole arm went rigid, and he laughed, but the laugh arrived late, like a subtitle out of sync. She did it again a frame later, harder, when he beat her score, and this time the red marks stayed.

Evan delivered the shoes to Dia, who was easy to talk to in a way that surprised him, and they bowled, and he threw two gutter balls in a row, which Dia found so funny she had to sit down on the ball return. "Your form," she managed, "is like a man falling off a ladder." He was, in spite of everything, having a good time, and the good time made the thing two lanes over harder to look at, because looking at it felt like interrupting something, like pointing at a stranger's stain. He kept thinking about the number. One in twelve was not rare. It was two kids in a classroom of twenty-four. It was not a malevolent stranger in a movie; it was somebody's girlfriend at a bowling alley on a Friday.

With twenty minutes before cosmic bowling, Evan made an excuse about the vending machine and walked over. Jaylen was alone at the moment, racking the pins.

"Hey," Evan said. "Weird question. You okay?"

"I'm winning, so, define okay."

"She grabs your arm pretty hard," Evan said, and then, because the sentence felt like an accusation, he added, "I just noticed."

Jaylen set the ball down. "She's competitive."

"I read this thing in Bouchard's class. CDC did a survey in 2021, Youth Risk Behavior Survey. Out of high schoolers who'd dated, about one in twelve reported physical dating violence." He heard how it sounded, like a pamphlet, and kept going anyway. "I don't know if that's this. I'm not saying it's this. I'm saying I'd rather ask badly than not ask."

Jaylen looked at his own forearm, where the marks had faded to pink. For a second Evan remembered being eleven, at this same alley, when Chad had dared him to bowl with his eyes closed and he had cracked a fingernail on the gutter and Chad had carried his shoes to the car without being asked, which was the closest thing to a model he had for what you did for a friend. Jaylen exhaled.

"She says it's a joke," Jaylen said. "It kind of started as one."

"Okay."

"I don't actually like it," Jaylen said, quieter, as though discovering this in real time. "I keep telling myself I don't mind, and then I mind."

The overhead lights dimmed, and the blacklights came on in a slow wash of violet, and Dia called from their lane, "Evan, your ball is staging a sit-in!" Jaylen rubbed his arm once, glanced toward the snack bar where his girlfriend was queueing, and picked up his ball again, but he stood there without throwing it.

"Sit with us for cosmic," Evan said. "There's room."

"Let me think for one frame," Jaylen said, and set the ball down on the rack, and watched the pins glow.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The booth by the window had become theirs by accident, three Saturdays running, and Leah had started to think of it as a place where hard things got said. She spread her notes across the table, covering the salt and most of the laminated menu, while Adrian slid in across from her and Mya balanced a phone against the napkin dispenser. On the wall behind Adrian hung a faded mural of montane forest, blue-green slopes stacked behind one another, which Leah fixed her eyes on whenever the Spanish left her entirely.

"Five minutes," Mya said. "Topic: should the city pay restitution to the neighborhoods it demolished for the reservoir. You take yes, Adrian takes no, and I time it. All Spanish. If you break into English, I restart the clock."

"That's brutal," Adrian said, but he was already flipping his own notes face down. He wanted the timing role last week and hadn't gotten it, and he wanted, Leah suspected, to beat her at something before the regional competition, where they would be paired instead of opposed. She couldn't blame him. She had beaten him at every practice round since September, and his pride had a visible weight to it lately, like a coat he couldn't take off.

Mr. Lin came over with water and the little pot of tea they always ordered whether they wanted it or not. He had coached the debate team years ago, before he bought the restaurant, and he had a habit of standing just long enough to hear one exchange before drifting back to the counter. Leah enunciated her opening sentence carefully, aware of him there, aware of the murmur from the other tables.

"La ciudad debe dinero a esas familias," she began, "porque..." And then it vanished. The word she wanted, the money the government takes from wages, the thing her whole second argument depended on. Tax. She had known it at eight o'clock this morning; she could picture the flashcard. Adrian's eyebrows lifted, waiting for her to fold, and the timer on Mya's phone glowed at eleven seconds.

She did not stop. "El dinero que el gobierno toma de su sueldo cada mes," she said, slow but level, "dinero que todas las personas pagan al gobierno, que la ciudad usó para construir el embalse." Adrian blinked. She kept going, riding the description like a plank across a gap, and by the time she reached the end of the sentence she had landed on the other side with her argument intact.

"Treinta y dos," Adrian said in Spanish, fighting her now, "because the payments ended and the law was clear." But he said it without his usual sharpness, and when her five minutes ended he leaned back and looked at her almost grudgingly. "You forgot the word."

"Obviously."

"And you just talked around it. For like fifteen seconds."

"It's called circumlocution," Mya said, lowering the phone. "We read about it in the linguistics thing for class. Describing a word you can't remember instead of stopping. It's a real strategy, it's in the textbooks. It keeps you talking."

Mr. Lin, wiping the next table, said nothing, but he was smiling at the mural as if it had told him something.

Leah sat with that. All season she had treated forgetting as failure, the way a dropped pass was failure, and she had drilled vocabulary the way other people drilled free throws. Now she turned the idea over: maybe the mark of speaking a language wasn't never stumbling but stumbling forward. She thought of her grandmother, who had learned English in this neighborhood and narrated around missing words her whole life, unembarrassed, telling whole stories about "the thing for the stairs that goes up and down on its own." Leah had always heard that as deficiency. She wasn't sure she still did.

But she wasn't sure she was entirely right, either. If she leaned on talking around words, would she ever learn the words themselves? Adrian seemed to be having a parallel thought, because he said, quietly, "If I did that, I'd fake it forever. I'd never learn tax." Then he looked up at her with something more open than competition. "Trade sides with me. You argue no, restitution is a mistake, and I'll argue yes. I want to see if I can do the talking-around thing when I forget, not just when you do."

She gathered her notes and squared them into a fresh pile, yes arguments pushed to the edge of the table, no arguments pulled close. Mya reset the timer. Out the window the afternoon light had gone long and gold across the street, and Mr. Lin was already coming back with the teapot.

"Empieza," Leah said.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Eva had the whole stage to herself for another forty minutes while the janitor ran his cart through the halls. She sat on the edge of the risers with her grandfather's guitar across her knees, a borrowed tuner clipped to the headstock, and a problem she hadn't expected: every string was wrong.

She had found the guitar two weeks ago, leaning in the back of her grandmother's closet behind a fur coat nobody wore anymore. Her grandmother had waved a hand and said take it, take it, he hasn't touched it since the surgery, and Eva had carried it home on the bus feeling like she was smuggling something alive. The strings were dark with old grease, the wood scratched pale at the sound hole where a wrist had rested for decades. But when she plucked the fattest string, the tuner's needle swung and parked itself at a letter that meant nothing to her yet, some flat murky nowhere below where it should live.

Tony had told her, in his loquacious way, half an hour of talking that could have been five minutes, that old guitars go out of tune all over, that the strings stretch, that the whole instrument forgets itself. "You have to teach it again from the beginning," he'd said, which sounded poetic until she was actually doing it and her fingers ached and the pegs resisted like small stubborn jaws. Heaven sat cross-legged on the stage a few feet away now, ostensibly working on a history essay, actually watching Eva with the tolerant amusement of someone who had already learned three chords and could not be told they were hard.

"Give me the phone," Eva said, and Heaven handed it over. Eva had found a chart in the school library, a diagram she'd photographed with the page number half in frame. Six lines, six letters. She'd expected the letters to make a word, something you could chant, and when they didn't she'd felt briefly cheated, as if the instrument had promised her a secret and delivered a shopping list.

She turned the low string's peg slowly, watching the needle drift. When it steadied on the E, the note came out round and full, and she understood something she couldn't have said out loud: that the letter wasn't a label, it was a location, a place the string belonged. She moved up. A on the next string, then D. The tuner's green light bloomed each time like a small approval. Somewhere in the middle strings the letters changed their spacing, G then B then back to E again, the same letter as the first but higher, a second city with the first city's name.

She remembered the summer she was eleven, driving with her grandfather through the savanna country east of the mountains, the grass gone gold and flat to the horizon. He had hummed the whole way, not songs exactly, just notes that wandered and found each other. She had asked him how he knew what to hum and he said he didn't, that the notes knew, and she had thought this was the kind of thing adults said when they didn't have a real answer. Now she turned the last peg, the thin one, until the needle centered on that high E, and all six strings, plucked one after another, fell into the order the chart promised, low to high, E A D G B E, and the wandering notes found each other the way his had.

The door at the back of the auditorium opened and Ms. Boateng came down the aisle with a stack of music folders, the drama teacher who also, inexplicably, kept a drum kit in the storage room. She paused at the front row. "That sounds like something now," she said. "Last week it sounded like a cat in a machine."

"Last week I didn't know the names of the strings," Eva said.

Ms. Boateng set the folders on the piano bench. "Play me all of them. Slow."

Eva pressed her sore fingers down and played the open strings from the bottom up, and in the empty auditorium the notes hung in the air and seemed to coagulate there, gathering into a real sound, a chord that wasn't a chord but was somehow still a kind of music. Heaven looked up from her essay. Somewhere above the stage a pigeon shifted on a beam and grit sifted down through the light.

"I still can't play anything," Eva said. "I can only tune it."

"That's the first thing that's true," Ms. Boateng said. "Everything else gets built on top of it." She checked her watch, then pointed at the folders. "Twenty minutes before rehearsal. Show me that bottom string again."

Eva turned the peg a fraction, listened, and plucked the low E one more time.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
story:
Camille had claimed the corner table by the window at the community art studio because the light there held steady all afternoon, and because from that spot she could see everyone without turning her head. Her project for the county show was due in nine days: a painting of her grandmother's kitchen, which meant deciding, before anything else, what colors the memory was allowed to have. She spread her swatches across the table, squares of cadmium yellow, cerulean, a brick red she had mixed herself and could not reproduce.

Yahya dropped into the chair opposite her, unwrapping a muffin he had no intention of sharing. "You're still on the swatches," he said. "You were on the swatches on Tuesday."

"It matters." She moved the yellow beside the red, then apart again. "The whole painting lives or dies here." Her grandmother's actual kitchen had been beige and tired, but she did not want to paint beige; she wanted the version that existed when you closed your eyes, warm and loud, the kettle always about to sing.

Mckenna arrived with wet hair and a truculent expression, having argued, apparently, with the vending machine. She set her charcoal down hard enough to make the jar of brushes jump. "It ate my dollar," she said. "So now I'm against all machines on principle." She leaned over Camille's shoulder, and some of the anger drained into curiosity. "Why are you arranging them in a circle?"

Camille looked down and realized she had done it without deciding to: the swatches bent into a ring, yellow flowing into green flowing into blue. "I don't know," she admitted. "It felt right. Opposite the red should be the green, and opposite the yellow, the purple." She tapped the empty spaces. "I've been fighting it, though. Half of me wants to plan it all out like this, and half of me wants to just start and let the kitchen tell me what it needs."

"That's a dialectic," Yahya said, pointing at her with the muffin. "Thesis, antithesis. Mr. Okonkwo drilled it into us second semester."

"It's not a dialectic, it's a Tuesday." But she kept turning the ring of colors, and something tugged at her, a lesson from somewhere half remembered. Then it surfaced whole. "Wait. You know where this comes from?" She pulled out her phone and typed with one thumb. "Isaac Newton. He arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle, in his book Opticks, in 1704." She turned the screen so they could see the old engraved disc, the colors marching around its rim. "The color wheel. Artists use it today. It started with a physicist."

Mckenna frowned at the image. "The gravity guy."

"The gravity guy." Camille sat back. "Which is honestly a little annoying. I wanted it to belong to painters. Some anonymous person mixing pigments for a cathedral wall." She turned the phone off and looked at her own crude ring, the torn edges of the swatches, the paint smudge on her knuckle. "But maybe it's better this way. He took light through a prism and bent it into a circle because the circle made sense of it, and three hundred years later I'm sitting here doing the same thing for a kitchen."

The studio's afternoon class began gathering near the kiln, and Mr. Okonkwo came through on his rounds, pausing at their table long enough to nod at the ring of swatches. "Good," was all he said, and moved on, which from him was effusive.

Camille worked while the light lasted. She did not resolve the argument between planning and instinct; she let the wheel stand as her map and then, choosing the cerulean for the window frame where no wheel would have sent her, painted one deliberate wrong thing. The blue captivated her more than she wanted to admit, cool against the brick red, not what memory said but what memory meant. She would decide tomorrow whether it stayed. For now she rinsed her brush, and the water in the jar swirled red, then yellow, then a muddy violet she could not name.

"Sixty more minutes," Mckenna said, checking the clock.

"Then I paint the kettle," Camille said, and picked the brush back up.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.
story:
The new warm-up appeared the first Tuesday of November, taped to the rink door in the trainer's tidy handwriting: single-leg hops along the boards, lateral shuffles, squat landings off the bench, all of it before anyone touched a puck. Audrey read it twice while lacing her skates, because the list looked like something a track team would do, not a girls' hockey team six weeks into its season. By the time the team formed a ragged line along the blue line, Corbin was already groaning, and Abigaelle had her stick balanced across her shoulders like a yoke, muttering that they were being turned into ducks.

"We're not even jumping in hockey," Corbin said, doing the hops anyway, badly, listing sideways each time she landed.

Mr. Chaudhry, who ran the pro shop and had somehow been drafted into supervising the routine while the trainer was away at a conference, watched from the gate with his arms folded. When Abigaelle asked him why they were doing this, he gave a noncommittal shrug, as though the whole business had been invented above his head, and said only that it was the program the association had sent out. He offered nothing further. Audrey, who suspected that adults who shrugged usually knew more than they admitted, decided to find out for herself.

She stayed after practice on Thursday, ostensibly to work on her wrist shot, and absconded with the folder Mr. Chaudhry had left on the bench when he went to sharpen a pair of skates. Behind the drill list was a printed page from the trainer, headed with a sentence Audrey read slowly, then again: neuromuscular warm-up programs, the ones that train balance, landing and cutting technique, have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. She sat with the page in the cold and the noise of the ice-resurfacer, hearing the words land one at a time. Balance, landing, cutting. Knee ligaments. She thought of her cousin, who had torn hers playing soccer at nineteen and spent a year learning to run again, and she thought of the hops she had been mocking all week, and she put the page carefully back in the folder before Mr. Chaudhry returned.

She did not announce what she had read. Partly this was because the team was in a mood, and any fact delivered by Audrey on behalf of the association would be received like a summons to detention. But partly it was because she wasn't sure the fact alone would convince anyone, herself included. It had convinced her, she realized, only when she connected it to her cousin's knee, and she couldn't hand that connection to Corbin like a pass.

Corbin noticed the change before anyone else did. On Saturday, Audrey did the whole routine without commentary, without the duck-waddle, without sighing at the squat landings; she even corrected Abigaelle's knee position on the lateral shuffles, tapping her own knee to show how it should sit over her foot. Corbin had spent the week treating the warm-up as a tax on her time, and now this, Audrey going quiet and diligent, unsettled her more than any lecture would have. She cornered her by the water bottles between periods.

"You're actually doing it," Corbin said. "Like, properly."

"Balance, landing, cutting," Audrey said. "That's the whole thing. It's a neuromuscular warm-up program, and it's been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries." She said it plainly, the way you'd report a score.

"Who told you that?"

"Nobody told me. I read it. I took the folder when Mr. Chaudhry wasn't looking." She glanced toward the pro shop, where he was running the till. "I put it back."

Corbin looked out at the ice, where Abigaelle was taking a draw and losing it, and where a girl on the other team had just cut hard to the net and gone down in a heap, getting up slowly, testing her leg. The rink went quiet in that particular way it did when everyone was watching one body to see what it would admit. The girl skated to her bench on her own, favoring the leg, and the play resumed.

Abigaelle skated over to the gate at the end of the period, sweating and curious, wanting to know what they'd been talking about. Corbin told her, in her own words, about balance and landing and cutting, about knees, about what the routine was apparently for, and Audrey listened to see how the fact survived the retelling. It survived fine, more or less, though Corbin added a flourish about the folder being stolen that made it sound like a heist. What Audrey still didn't know, and said so, was whether it would matter, whether six weeks of hops could really be weighed against the girl who had gone down on the far half-wall. Nobody answered, and when the buzzer sounded, Corbin pulled her helmet back on and was first through the gate.

"Stance first," she called over her shoulder, and Audrey followed her onto the ice.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
The rink smelled of scorched ice and burnt coffee, and by the second period Sebastian had claimed the spot where the heaters couldn't reach him, which was the spot where he could see the whole sheet of ice. His brother was playing left wing in the league final, and around Sebastian sat the whole scattered tribe of his family: his mother clutching a paper cup she never drank from, his grandfather with a scarf wound up to his chin, and Rhys and Kash one row down, sharing a bag of popcorn like gulls.

"You know," his grandfather said, during a whistle, "I remember the very first Super Bowl. Watched it like it was yesterday."

Sebastian had been half-listening, tracking his brother's line change, but the sentence snagged on something. He turned. "The first one?"

"Green Bay Packers against the Kansas City Chiefs," his grandfather said, nodding slowly, the way people do when a memory is being handled with both hands. "Thirty-five to ten. Beat them hollow. It was down in Los Angeles."

Kash leaned back over the seat. "You watched it?"

"Every minute of it."

Sebastian did the thing he always did with claims, which was to take them apart quietly before deciding whether to believe them. He knew the shape of the fact; it was one of those things that lived in the trivia drawer of his mind, right next to the periodic table and the capitals nobody quizzed him on. January 15, 1967. He looked at his grandfather's hands, at the scarf, at the way the old man's eyes had gone somewhere else entirely. Somewhere between that date and this date there wasn't much room. His grandfather would have been small. Small enough that a memory of watching the game and a memory of being told about the game could fold into each other and become the same memory.

He didn't say that. Not yet.

Rhys, who had been silent, slid down to sit beside him, offering the popcorn. "Your brother's line is getting hammered out there."

"They're fine," Sebastian said, and meant it, and watched anyway. His brother had gone down hard in the corner, and his mother's cup had crumpled slightly in her grip, and the boy got up, skated a slow circle, found his place at the blue line. Sebastian exhaled.

Here was his problem, and it was a real one. His grandfather was not a man who made things up. His grandfather drove two hours in the snow to see a ten-year-old's league final. He kept a taxonomy of small kindnesses, remembered every neighbor's dog, had once sat through four hours of Sebastian's piano recitals without complaint. If the old man said he remembered something, then something had happened; the question was only what. And Sebastian had spent enough of his life in rooms with boys like Kash, who could argue a hole in anything, to know how this would go if he argued. You could win and still lose something.

But there was also Rhys, quiet Rhys, who believed things too easily and got laughed at for it in class, and Sebastian had watched that happen without stepping in more times than he liked to count.

In the third period the home team scored twice in ninety seconds, and the rink came apart with noise. The kids who were autochthonous to this place, the ones who had practically been raised on the resurfacer fumes, stood on their seats, and the newcomers stood too because standing is contagious. His mother was shouting. His grandfather was on his feet with both hands above his head, and when the second goal light spun, he grabbed Sebastian's shoulder and shook it.

"That," the old man shouted over the horns, "is exactly how Green Bay felt. Like the whole building was yours."

Sebastian looked at him. He could interpolate the two games, set one inside the other, but that wasn't the same as knowing. "Grandpa," he said, carefully, under the noise. "The first Super Bowl was January of sixty-seven. That's, what, you would've been a little kid."

His grandfather considered this, and for a moment the rink roared on without either of them. "A little kid," he admitted. "My father had the radio on. I remember the kitchen, I remember the noise he made." He rubbed his jaw. "Maybe I wasn't watching. Maybe I was just there."

Rhys was watching them both. Kash was watching the puck.

"It still counts," Sebastian said.

The old man grunted, and adjusted his scarf, and turned back to the ice, where his youngest grandson was circling behind the net with the puck on his tape and the whole building rising to its feet.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse.
story:
The beaker in Sebastian's hands had gone cloudy in the wrong direction, and Zayan was watching it happen.

"That's backwards," Zayan said. "It's supposed to clear."

"It's not backwards. It's exactly what the data says." Sebastian set the beaker on the bench between their two stations. In Ms. Nolan's lab the afternoon light came in flat and grey through the high windows, and the heating plate ticked as it warmed the second sample. The colour deepened as the temperature climbed, the same deepening they had seen three times now, and Zayan's science fair board, propped against the wall with its tidy printed hypothesis, was quietly contradicted by every trial.

"You wrote that heat would push it forward," Sebastian said.

"Everyone knows heat speeds things up."

"Speeding up isn't the same as shifting." Sebastian pulled his notebook across the bench and turned it so Zayan could see the two columns he'd been keeping since Tuesday. "Forward reaction's exothermic. It gives off heat. So when you add heat from outside, the system can absorb it by running in reverse. The whole thing slides back toward the reactants. That's what we're looking at."

Zayan didn't answer right away. He picked up the beaker, tilted it toward the window, and put it down again with the careful movements of someone who had built a display board around being wrong. "So my prediction didn't fail because I measured badly."

"It failed because of the direction of the shift."

"That's worse."

Sebastian almost said something facetious about the fair, about how the judges on Saturday would love a board titled "I Was Wrong," but Zayan's shoulders were doing a thing Sebastian recognized from the semester they'd shared immunology notes, back when Zayan's marks had slipped and he'd stopped handing things in rather than hand in things that weren't first. He closed the notebook instead.

Rita came over from the fume hood with her own sample, still warm through the gloves. "Ms. Nolan wants to know if you two are presenting together or separately," she said. Then she saw the board, the beaker, the two columns. "Oh."

"It's a direction problem," Zayan said. "Not a data problem."

Rita looked at Sebastian, who found that the look carried a question he wasn't sure he could answer. He had spent two weeks on those columns, testing the shift at three temperatures, and somewhere in the middle of it he had stopped thinking of the equilibrium as a thing that obeyed him and started thinking of it as a thing that answered, in its own grammar, whatever question you actually asked. His first question had been sloppy. The answer had been honest anyway. He didn't know how to subsume Zayan's pride and his own certainty and Ms. Nolan's rubric under one clean conclusion, and he suspected the honest move was to say so.

"Separately," he told Rita. "But same data."

"You want to present data that contradicts his board?"

"I want to present what happened." He uncapped a fresh sample and set it on the heating plate beside the cooled one, so they could watch the shift move both ways. "We can show it. Cold, then warm, then cold again. It moves back. It's not a mistake, it's a system responding."

Zayan was quiet while the plate ticked up through thirty degrees. When the colour began to pale, reversing along the same path, he took the marker out of his bag and crossed out the hypothesis line on his own board, then wrote beneath it in small letters, "Forward is exothermic." He stood back and read it.

"Is that enough?" he said.

"It's the whole thing," Sebastian said.

Rita went to tell Ms. Nolan, and Zayan picked up the cold beaker and held it against his wrist like he was checking for a fever, watching the colour come back dark.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
The rink had been a grocery store before Mr. Levy bought it and flooded the floor, and the freezers still hummed behind the rental counter, giving the whole place a smell of old ice and cardboard. Cohen stood at the skate rental window with his hands in his jacket pockets, rehearsing. He had asked Jacqueline out on Tuesday, in the hallway outside the chemistry lab, and she had said yes so quickly that he had suspected, for one bad second, that she had not heard the question properly. Now she was late, seven minutes late, and the small worry in his chest had begun to metastasize into a full theory of the evening: that she had changed her mind, that the yes had been politeness, that he would skate alone for an hour and go home.

Then the door opened and she came through it with snow in her hair, apologizing about a bus, and the theory collapsed. He got her skates, size seven, and his own, and they went out onto the ice. He was better at this than she was, it turned out. He had come here with Kristopher all through middle school, before Kristopher got serious about hockey and moved to the real rink across town. Jacqueline clung to the boards for the first two laps, laughing at herself, and he skated backward in front of her, holding out a hand she refused with sardonic politeness, as though the hand were an insult she was choosing to forgive.

They bought hot chocolate at the counter, the kind from a machine that Mr. Levy had never once cleaned, and carried the paper cups back toward a bench by the boards. It was there that it happened. Cohen reached for his cup, and her elbow caught it, or his sleeve did, he honestly never worked out whose fault it was, and the chocolate went over the bench, over his sleeve, and in one long brown ribbon across the ice itself. He crouched with napkins. She stood with her hands over her mouth.

"Okay," she said. "Just so we're clear, that was your cup and your arm."

"It was gravity's fault," he said. "Gravity spilled it. We were both just standing near gravity."

"You're trying to make this not awkward and it's making it more awkward."

He stopped with the napkins halfway to the ice. Because he was not, in fact, trying to make it not awkward. Something Kristopher had told him last week, in the library, when Cohen had admitted he was terrified of the date, was sitting in his mind fully formed, and he decided, kneeling in a puddle of machine chocolate, that this was the moment to use it. "Kristopher told me about this thing," he said. "There was this experiment in 1966, by Elliot Aronson and some colleagues. They had this quiz contestant who was really competent, and at one point the contestant spilled a cup of coffee. And people rated him more likable afterward because of it."

"Because he spilled coffee."

"Because he spilled coffee. It's called the pratfall effect."

Jacqueline looked down at him, at the ruined napkins, at the brown smear freezing on the ice. From where she stood, the boy crouched at her feet looked suddenly younger than he had all evening, and also more real, the way a photograph of someone looks more real than the person smiling across a lab hallway. She had said yes on Tuesday partly because he seemed unbothered by everything, and unbothered had worried her a little, because she was bothered by most things and did not know how to be otherwise. Now here he was, reciting a psychology study from his knees in a rink that smelled like freezer burn, and she found she was glad, and she also suspected she was being managed.

"So you're saying," she said slowly, "that you read about a study, and then you told me the study, right after you spilled. On purpose."

"No. The spill was real. The telling was on purpose. Those are different things."

"Are they?"

They were back on the ice by then, skating side by side this time, her hand light on his arm. Mr. Levy came out with a mop for the chocolate and gave them a look that suggested spills were a personal offense, and Cohen skated a wide respectful arc around him. The rest of the hour went the way good hours go, unevenly. They raced and she fell and he helped her up and she said the pratfall effect was clearly working for her now too, and he laughed, and then for a while neither of them said anything, and the silence had an edge on it that neither of them mentioned. He knew what the edge was. She had asked whether his honesty was a contrivance, and he had said no, and the truth was closer to maybe, and they both knew it. He had wanted her to like him more, and the study had given him a way to want it out loud, and that was either the most honest thing he had done all night or the least, depending on how you counted.

At the door, taking off the skates, she said, "Same time next week?"

"Same bus, seven minutes late?"

"I'll aim for ten," she said, and handed him her rented skates to carry to the counter, which he did, and then he stood in the doorway watching her walk off down the salted sidewalk, still not entirely sure whether he had won anything or merely confessed.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Leo spread the two articles across his grandfather's kitchen table, on top of a cloth dusted with flour that never quite wiped away. One article claimed later school start times raised grades; the other claimed the effect vanished once you looked more carefully. Ms. Shapiro wanted a critical review that compared them, and Leo had spent three days circling the same paragraph like a dog before a closed door. His grandfather moved around the kitchen clattering the pasta machine, which was his way of offering help without offering help.

"Your grandmother wrote reviews," the old man said. "Book reviews. She once called a famous novelist a loquacious hamster and got away with it, because she proved it with quotations." He clamped the machine to the table edge and began feeding dough into the hopper. "Come, turn the crank. If you stare at those papers any harder, you will extrude conclusions like noodles, long and soft and without shape."

Leo took the crank. Thin ropes of spaghetti emerged from the bronze dies and swung gently, and he found that turning something with his hands let his mind turn too. His phone buzzed on the counter. Jacqueline had sent a photo of her own draft, six paragraphs long, and a message: "I picked the first article. It's obviously right. What's taking you so long?"
