"It's not obviously right," Leo typed back one-handed. "The second article says the first one only studied two schools."

"Then find out who's right," she wrote, which was exactly the kind of advice that sounded simple from someone whose grandfather did not own a pasta machine.

He cranked, and thought, and cranked. The disagreement felt personal, as if the two teams of researchers had chosen their conclusions first and then gone hunting for evidence to hold them up. What he wanted was a way to stand above both of them without pretending they were equal. That evening, after a dinner during which he and his grandfather reached a wary detente over whether Parmesan belonged on seafood pasta, Leo sat in the armchair by the window with his laptop and typed the question the way a tired person types: "all studies school start times grades what do they say together."

The result that came up first was not another single study. It was something that had gathered the studies themselves, dozens of them, and pooled what they found. Leo sat forward so fast the armchair squeaked. He read the page twice, then carried the laptop into the kitchen where his grandfather was washing the dinner dishes.

"It's called a meta-analysis," Leo said. "It combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can."

His grandfather dried his hands slowly. "So it is like tasting the whole pot instead of one spoonful."

"I guess. Yeah." Leo looked at the screen again. "Both articles are partly right, sort of, and both of them are arguing from pieces. The pooled effect is small. Small but there, probably. And even that might depend on things nobody measured, like whether the kids actually went to bed earlier." He laughed, a little stunned. "I've been trying to decide a verdict like a judge, and the honest answer is a shrug with a number attached."

"Write the shrug," his grandfather said. "Your grandmother made a career of it."

The next morning Aydin called, and Leo described the whole thing while watching his grandfather feed fresh dough into the machine for a second batch, this time fettuccine. "So you're not picking a side?" Aydin said. "Bold. Jacqueline is going to call you a coward."

"She already did. Then she read the meta-analysis and now she's rewriting her essay, and she's furious at me for being right first, so that's a nice change." Jacqueline had sent one more message overnight: "Fine. But you're proofreading mine." Leo had agreed, because a detente, he was learning, holds better when both sides give up something.

He wrote the review at the kitchen table between turns at the crank. He laid out what each article claimed, what each had genuinely found, where each had leaned too hard on too little, and then the pooled estimate and everything it could not tell him. His grandfather read the final draft aloud while the fettuccine dried on a rack, performing the sentences with great ceremony, pausing over the phrase "the limits of the evidence" as if it were poetry.

"There," the old man said at the end, tapping the page. "A loquacious hamster would have picked a winner. You did better." He slid the printed pages back across the floured cloth. "Now go put water on to boil. You have earned lunch."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale lists a change in residence as a stressful life event worth 20 points, the same as a change in schools.
story:
The moving truck was coming at eight in the morning, and by eleven that night the kitchen still had a wall of boxes with nothing written on their sides. Clara stood among them with a marker in her hand, uncapped, and wrote nothing.

"You're going to write nothing on every box," her mother said from the doorway. "That's a system too, I guess."

"It's a system of not deciding." Clara capped the marker. The house had already stopped being theirs in the legal sense; the buyers had signed that afternoon and asked, politely, whether the appliances would stay. Her mother had said yes to the stove and no to the washer, and Clara had stood in the hallway hearing her childhood negotiated in clauses, item by item.

She went upstairs and called Janice, who answered on the second ring because it was still early enough in the friendship that people answered fast.

"I found something," Clara said. She had found it at two that afternoon, procrastinating, scrolling with one hand while taping boxes with the other: the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, 1967, a list psychologists had once used to rank life events by weight. "Listen to this. A change in residence is worth twenty points."

"Points like a game?"

"Points like an illness. It's a stress scale." She turned her laptop toward the phone as if Janice could see it. "And here's the part. A change in schools is also twenty. The same. Moving house and switching schools are tied, and I'm doing both in one week, so."

"So you're basically sick," Janice said. "Clinically."

"Don't make it a joke."

"I'm not making it a joke, I'm externalizing it. That's what Ms. Marino calls it. Put the feeling outside yourself so you can look at it." Janice had absorbed a semester of psychology through Ms. Marino the way other people absorbed weather. "If the scale says it's real, then it's real, and you're allowed to be wrecked."

Clara looked at the strip of painter's tape on her wall where a poster had been for six years. "It doesn't feel like twenty points. It feels like arithmetic. Boxes times rooms plus mileage."

"Twenty plus twenty," Janice said. "Forty."

"Forty."

They were quiet for a moment, and then Janice said she had to go, and the shortness of the goodbye was the first thing all day that had actually hurt.

In the morning the movers came, and Clara's job was to stand at the truck and make judicious calls about what went where, which meant saying "That one's fragile" with authority she did not feel. The neighbor from two doors down, the one Felicity's family had feuded with over a fence for a decade, came out to watch with her coffee. She waved. It occurred to Clara that she had never once waved back.

At noon her father drove her to the new town, forty minutes east, so she could be registered before the district office closed at four. It was that or wait until after the move, and after the move she'd be unenrolled in one district and not yet enrolled in the other, which apparently made her, administratively, nobody. The deadline concentrated the mind wonderfully. In the parking lot she ate half a sandwich and did not finish it.

The registrar was a tired man with a lanyard, and he slid a form across the counter that asked for everything Clara had, including several things she had never thought of as possessions. Emergency contacts. Foreign languages. Honors. She wrote her name and then stopped at the line for extracurriculars.

"She's deciding," her father said. "She's a very judicious decider."

"Dad."

"Take your time," the registrar said, without meaning it.

There was a girl in the waiting area, maybe her age, filling out the same form with the speed of someone who had done it before, three times by the look of her overstamped folder. She caught Clara staring.

"Third school in two years," the girl said. "I'm a professional."

"First one," Clara said. "Ever."

"Oh, you're a rookie." The girl said it kindly, the way you'd say it to someone at their first day of a bad job. "Here's the only thing I know. Everybody acts like it's nothing. Pack a bag, make a friend, join a club. But I read that psychologists literally count it. Moving is on their stress list. Twenty points, same as changing schools, and I did both twice, so don't let anyone tell you you're fine."

"I know that scale," Clara said, and was surprised by how steady her voice came out. "Holmes and Rahe. I found it yesterday."

"Then you know more than my last guidance counselor." The girl went back to her form. Clara looked down at her own, at the blank line, and thought about forty points, and about Janice saying put it outside yourself so you can look at it, and about how both of those ideas were true at once: that the exhaustion had a number and a history, and that it was still hers to carry either way. She did not know yet whether the number made the thing lighter or heavier. She suspected it did both, depending on the day.

She wrote track, debate, and then, after a pause, added nothing else, and slid the form back across the counter.

Her father was already holding the door. Outside, the new street ran straight and long under a sky the color of unripe fruit, and somewhere down it a dog was barking at the movers unloading a house that was not yet theirs.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: An off-book rehearsal is one where actors must perform without their scripts, having memorised their lines.
story:
The community theatre smelled of dust and old paint, and the stage lights hummed in a way Sydney had stopped hearing until she stood alone in the empty house. She had taped out the set on the floor that afternoon, a rectangle of blue masking tape for the kitchen, a diagonal line where the door would be, and she had her notebook open to a page of arrows and initials. Mr. Balogun, who ran the youth one-act programme, had given her the slot on the condition that she direct, not just stage-manage, and she had said yes before she understood what the word would ask of her.

The first rehearsal went badly in a small, correctable way. Lochlan moved through the kitchen like a boy crossing a river on stones, pausing at each tape mark, and Douglas delivered her lines from the wing because Sydney had not told her where to stand. Sydney watched from the fifth row and realised that blocking was not a plan she imposed but a conversation she had to open, so she walked up onto the stage and put her hands on Lochlan's shoulders and turned him forty-five degrees toward where the audience would be.

"Try it from there," she said. "The line changes when you're not facing the wall."

It did change. Even Douglas, still clutching her script, looked up at the sound of it. They ran the scene four more times, and by the end Lochlan was moving through the kitchen as though he had always lived there, and Sydney felt something settle in her chest that was not pride exactly, more like the feeling of a key fitting.

At the second rehearsal she made her announcement. "Next Thursday we go off-book," she said. "Off-book means no scripts, lines memorised, the whole act."

Douglas said nothing, but the way she folded her script in half said plenty. By the following Thursday she had memorised perhaps a third of her lines, and when the scene reached its turn she stopped mid-sentence, stared at the taped floor, and said, "I don't know what comes next," in a voice so flat that Sydney understood it was not carelessness. Douglas had been working. The lines simply would not hold.

Sydney's first instinct was to be kind, to allay the panic she could see rising in Douglas's face by saying it was fine, they could stay on-book another week. Her second instinct, sharper, was the one she'd learned from Mr. Balogun's turgid little book of directing theory, the one that said a production keeps its calendar or it keeps nothing. She stood between the two for a moment, then asked everyone to take five, and sat down with Douglas on the edge of the taped kitchen.

"I set the date because I thought pressure was the point," Sydney said. "That's what the book says. That an off-book rehearsal forces you to find out where you actually are."

"I'm behind," Douglas said. "I know I'm behind."

"Do you want more time, or do you want to keep going and find the lines in the scene?"

Douglas looked at the folded script in her lap, then at Lochlan, who was pretending to stretch in the corner and not pretending well. "Keep going," she said. "But if I call line, someone says it fast. No faces."

So they kept going. Sydney called rehearsal back, took her seat in the fifth row, and watched Douglas reach for her lines and miss, and reach again and find them, whole passages surfacing as if the scene itself were hauling them up. When Douglas dried completely she said "line" the way they'd agreed, Lochlan fed it to her without looking up from his blocking, and she went on. It was not the performance Sydney had imagined, but it was something more useful, a true picture of what they had and what they still owed.

Afterward, in the lobby with the folding chairs stacked against the wall, Sydney tried to work out what she believed about what had happened. The date had mattered; without it, Douglas would have gone on believing she was further along than she was. But the harshness Sydney had been ready to offer as reparation for her own earlier softness would have gotten them nothing. Maybe the honest position was both at once, hold the line and forgive the misses, and maybe that was just a way of not choosing. She could not tell yet, and she wrote in her notebook, under the arrows and initials, "off-book Thursday, again," and turned off the last of the work lights. In the dark, Douglas's voice was still running the scene to herself, quietly, all the way to the parking lot.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome sat on top of the upright piano in the corner of the community center's music room, a pyramid of walnut with a brass pendulum, ticking out its patient arithmetic while Ella mangled the same eight bars of Chopin for the fourth time. It had belonged to somebody's grandfather, according to the sign taped to the lid, DO NOT MOVE, and it kept ticking even when nobody was playing, which Ella found faintly accusatory.

"You're rushing the left hand again," said Sarah-Maude, who was sprawled on the folding chair with her violin case across her knees. "The whole thing gallops when you do that."

"I know it gallops. That's the problem. I can hear it and I can't stop it." Ella put her hands in her lap and looked at the metronome the way she imagined people once looked at oracles. "Ms. Silva says I have two weeks to fix it or she's pulling me from the recital. Two weeks."

The recital was the community center's spring fundraiser, and Ms. Silva, who ran the music program on grant money and stubbornness, had made it plain that a galloping Chopin was worse than no Chopin at all. Ella had spent the whole school year earning her place in that program, taking two buses on Thursdays, and the thought of losing it over eight bars made her throat tight.

Brett wandered in late, as he always did, smelling faintly of the chlorine from the pool downstairs. "Is that thing still going? My mom says it's been in here since before the flood in the basement. Somebody told me once that Beethoven invented it, which is why it's so old."

"He didn't invent it," Ella said, and then stopped, because she realized she wasn't sure who had. She knew only what her grandmother had told her once, dusting the piano at home with a story attached: "Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815," Gran had said, tapping the little wooden case, "drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel." Ella had been eleven and had mostly cared that the tick sounded like a beetle in a wall. Now she said it out loud, the whole sentence, and Sarah-Maude raised an eyebrow as if Ella had recited a spell. It was strange what stuck and what didn't.

"So it's a stolen idea, kind of," Brett said, delighted.

"Patented off somebody else's design. It's complicated." Ella wound the weight down the pendulum and set it to largo, as slow as she could stand. "Which is basically my whole problem in musical form."

She practiced slow, and the slow was correct but lifeless, a Chopin who had given up. She practiced fast, and the fast was alive and wrong, the left hand sprinting away from the right like a dog slipping its leash. For three days she alternated between the two and got nowhere, and on Thursday Ms. Silva sat down beside her, listened to one pass, and delivered her verdict with the weary acumen of someone who had heard a hundred students fight the same fight.

"You think tempo is one thing. It's two things. There's the pulse you set, and there's the pulse you keep, and you've been treating them as the same enemy." She tapped the metronome's case. "Set it where the piece breathes. Then stop listening to the tick and start listening to yourself against it. Don't obey it. Check yourself with it."

Ella wanted to argue that this was the same advice dressed in nicer clothes, but she held her tongue, because she was sixteen and because it cost her nothing to try. That night she stayed after the center's pottery class let out, alone in the music room with the overhead lights buzzing and the metronome ticking away in the corner. The building was quiet except for the Saturday crowd, the usual sectarian squabbles over the small hall between the yoga group and the choir that had spilled into the corridors, someone's voice insisting they had signed the sheet first. Ella shut it all out.

She set the weight to the tempo where the melody actually sang, quicker than her safe slow, slower than her runaway fast. Then she played, and each time the left hand began to bolt she let the tick catch her, not as a command but as a question. Where are you now. Here. Where should you be. Here. It was exhausting in a way that running wasn't, the fatigue of holding two clocks in her head at once, the machine's and her own, and refusing to let either one win.

By the following Thursday she could get through the eight bars four times out of five. Sarah-Maude disabused her of the notion that this counted as solved: "The recital has people breathing and chairs scraping and Brett dropping programs. Your five bad times out of five will pick that day to show up." So Ella did something she'd been avoiding. She carried the metronome off the piano, Do Not Move be damned, and set it on the floor of the noisy lobby, right beside the sign-up table where the choir argued and the pool kids thundered past in flip-flops, and she played her eight bars there, badly at first, then less badly, the tick steady under the chaos like a hand on her shoulder that she could shake off whenever she chose.

On the night of the recital she played the Chopin with the metronome silent in the corner, watching her. The left hand bolted twice, and twice she gathered it back, and the ending was not clean but it was hers, shaped between the pulse she'd set and the one she'd learned to keep. Afterward Gran found her by the punch bowl, and Ella said, "You were right about that thing. Maelzel, 1815. Winkel's design." Gran smiled and said she'd never told Ella any such name, that she must have looked it up herself, and Ella stood there holding her cup, unable to decide whether she'd remembered a gift or invented one. Behind them, in the music room, the pendulum swung on.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: A 2008 trial in Norway found that young female soccer players aged 13 to 17 who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall.
story:
The clipboard felt heavier than it should have, considering it held one page. Elliot had spent Sunday night building the week: Monday intervals, Wednesday easy miles, Friday strides, and rest days slotted in like deliberate absences, which was the part that still felt wrong to him. Rest, in his old thinking, had been what happened when you failed. Mr. Ortiz had said only one thing about it, tapping the blank squares on the grid, that the empty days were the ones doing the repair, and then he had walked off to time the sprinters, leaving Elliot to believe it or not.

By Tuesday the track was loud with soccer players cutting across the infield, and Lorelei was among them, taping her ankle against the fence. Elliot crouched beside her because she was the one who had told him, last spring, that warm-ups were for people who didn't train hard. Now she was out for three weeks with a pulled hamstring, and she was the fastest girl either of them knew.

Patience found him at the water jug. She had the other clipboard, the team's, and she was running for captain in the fall vote. "You're the one with the spreadsheet," she said. "Come talk to my girls."

"I run track."

"You plan training. They don't listen to me because I want something from them. You don't want anything."

She wasn't wrong about the first part. The soccer girls had voted down the structured warm-up twice, ten minutes of drills before practice, because it was boring and because it cut into scrimmaging. Patience stood in front of them at the far turn and held up her hand for quiet, and when it didn't come, she waited, which was apparently a thing you could do with authority. Then she said it plainly, as if reciting something she had made herself memorize: "A 2008 trial in Norway found that young female soccer players aged thirteen to seventeen who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall."

"Overall," someone repeated, meaning so what.

"Overall," Patience said. "Not just knees. Everything."

One of the girls, the keeper, said ten minutes was ten minutes. Another said Norway, like the word itself was an argument against it. Elliot watched Patience absorb this, wanting it too visibly, and he understood that her teleology, if you could call it that, was the vote in September, every good idea bent toward getting elected. His own wanted object was stranger. He wanted a week on paper that would hold, a plan he could point to when something went wrong, and he could admit to himself that this was partly superstition.

"Show me the program," he said to her quietly, and she handed him the laminated sheet. It looked like homework. It looked, honestly, gratuitous in its complexity, all those numbered stations, when the girls' actual habit was four minutes of jogging and a conversation. He turned it over, thinking about his own grid, the way rest days only made sense once you trusted the plan as a whole. Maybe the warm-up was the same kind of thing, one part that looked pointless from inside a single day.

So when the keeper said prove it, Elliot didn't argue. He marked out the drills with cones on the infield while Patience ran the numbers on her fingers out loud, and the girls went through it once, badly, laughing at the hopping patterns, and then a second time, less badly. Lorelei watched from the fence with her taped ankle propped on a bag, and when the session broke up she waved him over.

"I did the warm-up," she said. "Every practice, all spring. Patience has it backwards if she's telling you I skipped it." She looked at the flat gray sky above the scoreboard. "I still pulled the hamstring. Third week of the season."

Elliot stood there with the cones under his arm and let that sit between them, because anything he said next would be a lie of comfort. A third fewer injuries was not none. He had built rest days into his week believing they instantiated some law of training, and Lorelei had done everything right and was still sitting on a fence in April, watching other people run. Patience was already across the infield, collecting signatures or promises, and Mr. Ortiz was calling the mile group to the line.

"Write me a rehab week," Lorelei said. "You're the one with the spreadsheet."

He said he'd have it Friday, with the rest days marked, and he went to get his spikes.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
Mr. Sharma set the kitchen timer on the desk and Jackson's stomach dropped at the small plastic click. Twelve minutes until his turn. The debate topic was on the board in Spanish, school uniforms, and the rule was on the board too, underlined twice: five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no English.

"You practiced?" Nathanial asked. He had already gone, had lasted four minutes and eleven seconds before the word "however" came out in English and Mr. Sharma's pen moved on the clipboard.

"Some," Jackson said. His note card had eleven phrases on it, written small, and half of them were arguments against uniforms, which was not the side he had drawn. That was the problem, or the first problem. He actually supported uniforms, mildly, for reasons he could not yet say in Spanish, and he had been assigned to oppose them, and somewhere in the shower that morning he had begun to think the opposition had the better case anyway, or at least the more interesting one, and now he could not remember which belief was his and which was the assignment's.

Coen leaned across the aisle. "When you freeze, don't stop. Just say y luego, like, 'y luego...' and buy yourself a second."

"That's stalling."

"That's surviving."

Jackson ran his opening sentence in his head. En primer lugar, los uniformes no resuelven los problemas reales. He had it, he had the whole first minute, and then the second minute was an argument about cost, el costo, and the third minute he had planned to concede something, to say uniforms were not the worst idea, which his father called litotes and said was how you sounded fair when you were winning. Jackson had liked that. Say the other side is not entirely wrong, then land hard.

The girl at the front desk stood up for her turn. Jackson mouthed his opener again and it dissolved. He heard the word "presupuesto" and lost "in the first place" entirely, and what surfaced in his head, whole and fluent and useless, was English: the real issue is conformity. He pressed his thumbnail into the note card until it creased.

"My turn's after her," he said. "I'm going to blow it."

"You're going to code-switch," Nathanial said. "Everybody does. It's moving between two languages in one conversation. Doesn't mean you're bad at this."

Mr. Sharma looked up from the clipboard. "Focus, por favor."

Jackson stared at Nathanial. "That has a name?"

"It's not a crime, is what I'm saying. It's common. People who are actually fluent do it." Nathanial shrugged, a little petulant, like he'd been waiting all period for someone to ask him something he knew. "Doesn't mean you're bad at this," he said again, quieter.

It did not help the way Jackson wanted it to. The rule was still the rule, five minutes, entirely Spanish, and the timer did not care what was common. But something loosened anyway. He stopped trying to hold the whole argument in Spanish in his head like water in his hands, and started building it in both languages, English thought, Spanish sentence, and when the English word was the honest one, he circled it on the card and looked for its cousin. Conformidad. He knew that word. He had known it since October.

The girl at the front sat down at four minutes thirty. Mr. Sharma reset the timer, and the class got quiet in the way rooms do when everyone is relieved it is not them.

"Jackson. Cinco minutos."

He stood. "En primer lugar," he said, and his voice did the shaking thing and then stopped doing it. "Los uniformes no resuelven los problemas reales." He got through the cost argument, got to the part where he meant to concede, and there, in the third minute, under the pressure of the watching room and the ticking plastic, it happened: "the real issue is," and he heard it, the English sitting in the middle of his Spanish like a stone in a stream.

Mr. Sharma's pen hovered.

"La cuestión real," Jackson said, "es la conformidad." The pen settled back down. He kept going. Somewhere in the fourth minute he stopped reading the card and started arguing with the room, actually arguing, the position he had half-made and half-been-given, and he found he could not fully separate the two, and he said so, in Spanish, badly: "Quizás tengo razón, quizás no." Maybe he was right, maybe not. The timer went off with eleven seconds left on his last sentence and he finished it anyway, standing there, out of breath.

Mr. Sharma made a mark on the clipboard and did not say what it was. Coen mouthed "y luego" at him from across the room, grinning, and Nathanial slid a folded note across the aisle as Jackson sat down. Inside, in English, in the middle of a Spanish class, it said: not bad.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Recipients in an email's Bcc field are hidden from everyone else, which is why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use Bcc to protect their addresses.
story:
The volunteer office smelled of toner and cold coffee, and Ms. Rossi was typing with two fingers when Tristan knocked on the open door. She waved him in without looking up. On her monitor, half-visible from where he stood, was an email addressed to what looked like every parent in the district, the To field a long gray column of names he recognized from the graduation fundraiser list. Fifty of them, he guessed, maybe more.

"I need your help with the thank-you letters," she said. "You write better than I do, and the committee wants something with structure. An opening that states the purpose, a middle with the numbers, a closing that asks for one specific thing." She turned the screen toward him. "I've drafted the body. You do the rest."

He read it. The body was fine, direct and organized, but his eye kept going back up to the To field. He knew those addresses belonged to parents who, in most cases, had never met each other. His own mother's was third on the list, and he thought of her inbox, how carefully she guarded it after the year the school newsletter got forwarded to a chain of strangers and the spam started arriving like weather.

"Ms. Rossi," he said, "before you send this. Everyone in the To field can see everyone else's address."

"That's the point, isn't it? Transparency."

"There's a difference between transparency and handing out people's contact information without asking." He kept his voice flat, because she responded better to flat. "Bcc hides recipients from everyone else. That's why a message to a long list of people who don't know each other usually goes out that way, to protect their addresses. You put your own address in To, and everyone else in Bcc."

She sat back. "Half the committee would call that secretive."

"Half the committee can argue it at the meeting on Thursday."

Dominik was leaning against the filing cabinet by then, waiting for his community-service sheet to be signed, and he laughed. "Secretive. Like it's state business. It's a fundraiser, Tristan."

"It's fifty people who didn't agree to have their addresses circulated."

"So circulate them." Dominik shrugged. "I'm making a list for the prom committee, vendors, the whole parent network. This saves me three weeks of phone calls." He said it lightly, the way he said everything, as though wanting something were the same as being owed it, as though a person's inbox were common property a committee could expropriate whenever convenience asked.

Tristan felt the argument sharpen in him and made himself hold both halves of it. The school did need parents talking to each other; the fundraiser had survived on exactly that web of acquaintances, and Ms. Rossi was right that a contact list nobody could see could curdle into distrust. But there was a line between a community that shared things and one that was simply harvested, and Dominik was describing the second while calling it the first. What Tristan could not settle, even privately, was where the line actually sat, or who got to draw it. He thought of Keziah's mother, who had changed her email twice since September for reasons Keziah never explained.

"You can ask them," he said finally. "Bottom of the email. One sentence. If you'd like to be added to a shared parent contact list, reply yes. Then anyone who says yes is in, and anyone who says nothing stays private."

"A checkbox solution," Dominik said. "Penurious. You're rationing community."

"I'm rationing other people's personal information, which is not ours to spend."

Ms. Rossi looked between them, then deleted the To field, retyped her own address, and pasted the fifty names into Bcc without another word. "Draft the closing line," she said to Tristan. "And Dominik, if the prom committee wants contacts, they'll ask, in writing, and they'll take no for an answer." She signed his sheet and slid it across. Dominik pocketed it, still grinning, and left.

Keziah found Tristan in the corridor ten minutes later, holding her phone. "You'll want to see this. My mom got the thank-you email. First one she's opened all year." She turned the screen toward him. "She replied yes."

Below it, in the thread, a second reply had already appeared from a parent Tristan didn't know, and then a third, parents introducing themselves to each other, one small paragraph apiece, each of them asking before offering an address, each of them sounding, for the first time, like people who had chosen to be found.

"See you Thursday," Keziah said, and walked off toward the gym.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Some leases require the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covers the tenant's own belongings rather than the building and adds a monthly premium.
story:
The two leases lay side by side on the kitchen table, one from Marchand Court and one from a building on Felton Street, and Alice had been reading them long enough that the words had begun to look like weather. She was eighteen, she had a job at the library starting in September, and she had until Friday to tell the Marchand manager yes or no. Her mother moved behind her at the stove, stirring something with onions, and the kitchen smelled like a decision being postponed.

"You've read that one three times," her mother said.

"Because the third time it said something different." Alice tapped the page. The Felton Street apartment was twelve dollars cheaper each month, but heat was not included, and when she had called the utility office the woman there had said to budget conservatively, that an old building in winter could surprise you. So she had made two columns in her notebook, rent plus electric plus heat, and Marchand was winning by a margin she didn't trust because it was small and she had invented part of it.

Mercedes came over after her shift, still in her café apron, and sat down across from Alice with the seriousness of someone invited to judge a contest. She read the Marchand lease first because it was shorter, and her finger stopped halfway down the second page. "Here. What's this part."

Alice leaned in. The clause was two sentences, buried between rules about garbage and rules about guest parking. It required the tenant to carry renter's insurance for the whole term of the lease.

"Insurance for what?" Mercedes asked.

"For the building, I guess. If I burn it down." Alice said it lightly, but something in her chest had already gone quiet and careful. She read the clause again. It didn't say anything about the building. It said it covered her belongings, her own things, in her own rooms. She sat back and let that metabolize, the way a small fact can rearrange an entire afternoon. She had not once, in three readings of this lease, understood what she was agreeing to carry.

Vanessa, when they called her, was walking home from practice and winded. "My sister had that," she said over the phone's small speaker. "Renter's insurance. It covers your stuff, not the building. The landlord's insurance does the building. That's why it's a separate thing you pay for." Alice wrote it down while Mercedes watched her write it. It was one more line in the column, a premium every month, and it was not optional. She looked at her notebook and the numbers stopped matching what she'd promised herself.

"It's not a scam," Alice said slowly, testing the sentence. "It's just a cost I didn't know was a cost." Mercedes argued that twelve dollars cheaper was twelve dollars cheaper, heat or no heat, and Vanessa, still breathing hard down the line, said that old buildings in winter could turn any budget into a revisionist account of itself, all the numbers rewritten in hindsight. Alice laughed at that, but she kept the pen moving. She added the premium to Marchand's column, then, out of fairness, called Felton Street and asked whether their lease required it too. The manager said no, it wasn't in their lease, but she could carry it if she wanted to. That answer felt like a trap she couldn't see the shape of.

In the end the columns came out nearly level, Marchand slightly higher with the premium, Felton slightly higher with the heat, and the difference between them smaller than what she spent on coffee in a month. What she kept returning to was not the arithmetic. It was that she had almost signed a contract while misunderstanding its plainest clause, and that the correction had come from her own rereading, a friend's finger on a page, a sister's secondhand knowledge, all of it pooled. She closed the notebook, then opened it again and drew a third column, empty, headed with a question mark. Some things stayed uncertain, and she was starting to think that was not the same as being unprepared.

Her mother set a bowl of the onion stew in front of her, and Mercedes reached over and tore a piece of bread in half without asking.

"So which one is it?" Mercedes said.

Alice looked at the two leases, at the question mark, at the steam rising off the bowl, and pulled the Marchand lease toward her. "I'm going to sleep on it. But at least now I know what I'm sleeping on."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Sonata form has three main sections: the exposition presents the themes, the development works them through other keys, and the recapitulation brings them back.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and cold coffee, and Nevaeh had spread the Mozart score across the tailgate of Drew's mother's car because it was the only flat surface the band hadn't claimed. Three sticky notes sat in her pocket like small coloured flags: pink, blue, yellow. The portable speaker on an upturned milk crate had died twenty minutes ago, which meant she was marking the movement from the page alone, hunting for where themes appeared, vanished, and came back.

Around her, Drew's band was assembling drums and arguing about a set list for Friday. Charley tuned a bass guitar with the patience of someone who had done it a thousand times, and Nevaeh kept losing her place on the score every time a string snapped sharp.

"You could go inside," Drew said, not unkindly.

"The concert's Thursday," she said. "Ms. Bennett wants the score marked before we play it. First years who show up with a clean score get lectured at." She laid the pink note at the opening bars, where the first theme stepped out plainly in the tonic key. Then she flipped pages, following the second theme into a different key, and pressed the blue note there. Somewhere after that, she reasoned, things would break apart and wander through other keys before returning. She set the yellow note at what felt like a good place, two thirds of the way through, and sat back.

Charley wandered over between songs, wiping rosin dust from his hands. "What's the yellow one?"

"That's where the themes come back," she said. "The recapitulation."

He leaned in, and she watched his eyes travel the staves the way he read chord charts, left to right, no skipping. "Why there? I'd have put it after this double bar. See, everything before it you get twice with the repeat sign, and after the bar the music goes somewhere strange first." He tapped a passage where the key signature seemed to dissolve, the harmony sliding through keys she couldn't name. "That's where it wanders. Then your themes walk back in, what, here?"

Nevaeh looked. He was right about the wandering. She had followed chronology instead of function, placing the yellow note where the pages felt late rather than where the music actually came home. She peeled it off, the paper losing a little of its stick, and moved it to the return of the first theme, back in the tonic, unmistakable now that she knew to listen for it. "Exposition presents the themes," she muttered, half to herself, touching pink, then blue, "development works them through other keys, recapitulation brings them back." The sentence had the shape of the movement itself.

"I have no idea what that means," Charley said, "but it sounds like something my grandmother would say about a recipe."

Then Drew started the new song without counting anyone in, and Nevaeh, packing up, stopped with the score half in her bag. The song began with a melody stated plainly, twice. Then the band broke it apart, the bass dragging it through a key that made her teeth ache, the drums dismantling it bar by bar, until the melody reassembled itself near the end, recognisable but heavier, like someone returning from a long trip to the same front door.

"You wrote that on purpose?" she asked, when it ended.

Drew shrugged. "It's just how it goes. Verse thing, then we mess around, then the verse thing again but bigger."

Nevaeh laughed, then felt something in the laugh go thin and diaphanous, like the feeling might tear if she handled it. She had spent three evenings with this Mozart while her friends were becoming a band, and now the band had arrived at the same architecture without knowing its name, the way rivers arrive at the sea without a map. Maybe the form wasn't a rule you learned so much as a pattern that ossified out of hundreds of pieces, something the music kept choosing. Or maybe Drew's song was a coincidence, three parts because three parts is what songs do, and she was seeing her homework in everything like a face in plaster. That part she couldn't settle, and she let it stay unsettled.

At the door she turned back. "Thursday, after the concert, the garage. I want to hear the middle part again, the part that wanders."

Drew was already restringing, and Charley smiled at her over the bass. "Bring the sticky notes," he said. "Everything in here gets labelled eventually."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
story:
Elijah found the chemistry exhibit on the museum's second floor, past the hall of boreal dioramas where stuffed caribou stood frozen mid-step behind glass. Brock was already there, leaning over a mock lab bench with a worksheet in one hand and a pencil he wasn't using in the other. Their chemistry teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, had given the class free rein of the museum for the afternoon and stationed himself near the periodic table mural, answering questions only if asked directly, which was his way of pretending he wasn't supervising anyone.

"You did the methane one yet?" Brock said. He slid the worksheet across the bench. The problem asked how many moles of water formed from burning eighteen grams of methane. Brock's answer, circled twice, was something enormous, a number that would have filled a swimming pool.

Elijah read it twice. "How'd you get that?"

"Eighteen grams, and the equation says one methane to two water, so thirty-six grams, and grams to moles is just moving a decimal or whatever." Brock shrugged. He was the kind of student who finished first and defended the answer on the grounds of having finished first.

Kamryn came over from the tesla coil display with her own sheet. "Mine's different," she said, and held it up. Her answer was small, a little over two moles, and Brock looked at it the way he looked at scores that beat his.

Mr. Okonkwo drifted closer but stopped at the drinking fountain, taking his time. Elijah knew the maneuver. He'd watched the coach at basketball practice do the same thing, pretending to retie a shoe while a fight sorted itself out.

Elijah pulled the worksheet toward himself and started over in the margin. He wrote the balanced equation the museum had posted above the bench: methane plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water. One, two, one, two. Then he converted Brock's eighteen grams of methane into moles first, using the molar mass printed on the periodic table mural, and only after that did he touch the coefficients.

"Wait," Brock said. "You're converting before you use the ratio."

"You can't use grams in the ratio," Elijah said. He said it slowly, because he was testing it as he said it. "The coefficients in a balanced equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses." He looked at the numbers on the mural, then at his margin work, then at Kamryn's sheet. Two moles of water for every one mole of methane. His answer came out matching hers to the second decimal.

Brock leaned over and compared them side by side. He was quiet for a second, which for Brock was a long time. "So I turned grams into grams into moles, and the grams were never in the right ratio anyway."

"You counted grams like they were moles," Kamryn said. "Moles aren't grams. That's the whole trick."

"It's not a trick," Elijah said, though he wasn't sure that was right either. It felt less like a trick and more like a rule of the road, the way a city ordinance tells you which side of the street to park on. Nobody explains the ordinance; you just find out when you get the ticket. Brock had gotten the ticket.

Brock erased his circled answer, and the eraser smeared graphite across the page in a gray streak. "Fine. So all these problems, I've been doing them wrong since September?"

"Some of them," Kamryn said. "The ones where the masses happened to be equal to the moles, you got lucky."

Brock turned his pencil around and tapped the eraser end against the bench. He didn't say anything about September's test, the one he'd scored two points above Elijah on, but Elijah thought about it, and he suspected Brock knew he was thinking about it. The subtext sat between them like a third worksheet neither had picked up.

A museum docent announced that the planetarium show would begin in ten minutes, and Mr. Okonkwo finally left the drinking fountain. He glanced at Brock's smeared page on his way past and raised one eyebrow at Elijah, who raised one back. Mr. Okonkwo had once told the class that he could disabuse them of any misconception if they insisted on holding it, but that they'd remember better what they'd dismantled themselves. At the time Elijah had thought it was a way of avoiding work. Standing here now, with Brock reworking the problem from the top and Kamryn checking each line, it seemed more like a bet the teacher had placed and left on the table.

Elijah looked down at his margin again. He trusted the answer; the units had cancelled the way they were supposed to, and the numbers matched Kamryn's. Still, somewhere in the back of his mind a small doubt persisted, a suspicion that there was a version of this where the masses did matter and he'd meet it on the next worksheet unprepared. He decided he'd look at the next problem in the car, before Brock could finish it.

"Planetarium," Brock said, standing. He tore the worksheet off the pad and folded it into his back pocket. "You two can fight over who reads the answer aloud to Okonkwo."

"He already saw it," Kamryn said.

"He saw yours." Brock pointed at Elijah's margin work. "He doesn't know if I fixed mine."

Elijah picked up his pencil and started on the second problem.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The letter from Aldermere had been sitting in Paige's backpack for two days, unopened, because opening it would mean deciding something, and deciding something would mean admitting that the deciding had already happened somewhere inside her without permission. Now she sat in the guidance office under a poster that said YOUR FUTURE STARTS HERE in a font chosen by someone who had clearly given up, waiting for Ms. Tesfaye to finish with a sophomore whose crisis involved a stolen lacrosse stick.

"Penny for them," Ms. Tesfaye said when the door finally closed, which Paige had always found backward, since her thoughts were worth considerably less than a penny lately and cost considerably more to share.

"I got a likely letter," Paige said. "From Aldermere. They want me to apply Early Decision." She set the envelope on the desk between them like evidence at a trial, although she wasn't sure whether she was the prosecution or the defense.

Ms. Tesfaye picked it up, turned it over, said nothing, which was her way of making students do the work. It was a quality Paige both admired and resented, the way you admire a crosswalk that makes you wait.

The thing was, Paige had done her research, or enough of it to be dangerous. Early Decision was binding: if Aldermere admitted her, and the financial aid they offered was acceptable, she had to enroll and pull every other application. She had read the words on their website at one in the morning, her face lit blue by the laptop, her mother asleep down the hall after a shift that ended at eleven and a budget spreadsheet that never quite closed the gap. Binding meant no comparison shopping. It meant accepting whatever aid one school offered without ever seeing what another school might have put on the table.

Last spring, she and Steven had gone to a college fair in the gymnasium, and she could still see him at the table for a small liberal arts school in Ohio, expostulating with the recruiter about whether their merit scholarships stacked with need-based grants. "You can't just say 'it depends,'" Steven had said, palms up, delighted with his own outrage. "Everything depends on something. That's not information." The recruiter had laughed and given them both pens. Steven had applied nowhere yet, on principle, which Paige suspected was a mercurial form of fear dressed up as strategy, though she loved him anyway.

"Your mother's take?" Ms. Tesfaye asked now.

"She says it's my decision. Which means she's terrified. She thinks I'll turn it down because of money and spend my whole life apologizing to myself, or take it and spend my whole life apologizing to her." Paige had noticed, somewhere around October, that her mother's face did this complicated thing whenever Aldermere came up, a hopefulness that tried to flatten itself out before it could be witnessed, like a cat smoothing its ears.

There was also Leandro, who had texted her that morning: "ED is a loophole for people who can afford certainty." She had typed three rebuttals and deleted all of them, because he wasn't entirely wrong and because arguing with Leandro was like arguing with weather. He was applying to eight schools, all regular decision, all with aid calculators open in separate tabs, an apportionment of risk so careful it was almost its own kind of faith.

"I think I keep pretending the two of them are the only options," Paige said slowly, watching her own hands flatten the envelope's corner against the desk. "Steven thinks you chase the thing. Leandro thinks you protect yourself. And I've been standing in the middle doing an impression of a thoughtful person."

"And now?"

"Now I think the middle is a real place, actually, not just a dodge." She had worked it out in the shower that morning, where she did her best thinking, the steam and the white noise turning her brain mercifully slow. She could call the financial aid office and ask them to estimate her package before she applied. It wasn't the same as real offers from real schools. The estimate could be wrong; "acceptable" could turn out to mean something narrower than she'd hoped; she might still be gambling on a single number. But it was a way of binding herself with her eyes open, which was different from binding herself blind. She might be wrong to do it even so. She might spend next April thinking about the schools she'd never hear from. She was honest enough with herself to know she couldn't rule that out, only to decide it was a risk she could carry.

Ms. Tesfaye slid a sticky note across the desk. On it she had written the direct line for Aldermere's aid office and, beneath it, "Ask for the estimator. Get it in writing."

"That's it?" Paige said. "You're not going to expostulate about my future?"

"I expostulate about deadlines," Ms. Tesfaye said, standing to open the door. "Futures I just witness. Phone's in the hall, use the one by the trophy case, nobody's called home from it since 2011."

Pa gathered her backpack, then turned back and took the envelope out, setting it on the corner of the desk where she could see it while she dialed. She didn't open it. The envelope could wait; it had already waited two days, and it seemed, in its patient institutional way, prepared to wait a little longer. She picked up the receiver, heard the dial tone, and began pressing the numbers off the sticky note, one by one, while outside the window somebody's younger sibling wandered across the parking lot with a stolen lacrosse stick held high like a scepter.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product a reaction can make.
story:
The kitchen smelled of toast and burnt butter, and Anthony had the chemistry book propped against the sugar jar like a suspect under interrogation. His mother had left for her shift, the toaster was still warm, and the loaf of bread on the counter was down to its heel.

He was supposed to convert grams into moles, and the numbers refused to mean anything. Molar mass, the book said, was the bridge: grams of reactant, divided by grams per mole, gives moles, and moles of product follow from the equation. He copied the steps onto a napkin, then copied them again on a fresh napkin, as though a cleaner surface might make the arithmetic confess. He sat still and let himself cogitate, turning the whole thing over without touching the pencil, which was how he sometimes caught what he'd been missing.

Tony arrived first, letting himself in the way he did, and went straight for the cabinet. "Briana's coming. She says Mr. Navarro moved the quiz to Thursday."

"That's two days."

"That's two days," Tony agreed, and set out four slices of bread.

Briana came in with her notebook already open, and she began building sandwiches with the seriousness of someone performing a lab. Ham, cheese, ham, cheese. On the fourth sandwich she stopped, holding a slice of cheese over the bread with nothing beneath it.

"We're out of bread," Tony said.

"But there's cheese left," Briana said. "Half a package."

Anthony looked at the plate: four sandwiches, and the leftover cheese sitting there useless, unable to become anything. Something clicked open in his head, quietly, the way a jar finally gives.

"How many sandwiches could we make if we had more bread?" he asked.

"With this much cheese? Six, maybe seven."

"So the bread decides. Not the cheese, even though there's extra. The bread runs out first and it sets how many sandwiches you can make." He was already flipping to the chapter on stoichiometry. "That's it. That's what the book keeps saying. The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product a reaction can make."

"Congratulations," Briana said, biting into the evidence. "You've discovered lunch."

He hadn't, though, and he knew it. He'd discovered the shape of the idea, the way his father could describe a house without being able to build one. On paper it was grams and molar masses, and the grams didn't arrange themselves into sandwiches. He wrote the practice problem out: so many grams of one reactant, so many grams of another, and a question about grams of product. He found the moles of each by dividing by molar mass, then compared them against what the equation demanded, and made himself slow down at the comparison, because that was where he'd gone wrong the night before, in the dark, guessing.

"Talk it out," Briana said. "Mr. Navarro says talking it out works."

"That's metacognition," Anthony said. "Thinking about how you're thinking. He said that word about six times on Monday." He pointed his pencil at the two mole amounts he'd calculated. "This one's smaller than I need for all of the other reactant. So this one runs out first. It's the bread."

"So the product can't be more than what the bread allows," Tony said, mouth full.

"Right. The greatest amount of product is set by whichever runs out first." He carried the number forward, multiplied by the ratio from the equation, multiplied by the molar mass of the product, and got a grams answer that matched the back of the book. He checked it a second time, not because he doubted the arithmetic but because matching answers sometimes happened by accident, and he wanted to know he'd built the road rather than stumbled into the town.

Tony leaned over his shoulder. "You look sagacious."

"I look like a guy with a napkin."

"A sagacious guy with a napkin."

Then Briana turned her notebook around, and Anthony saw the problem she'd been working silently beside him, the same setup but with different masses, and her answer was nearly double his on a nearly identical problem. They compared lines. Her division was right. Her molar masses were right. She had simply carried forward the reactant that was still sitting in surplus, the cheese, the one that ran out second, and let it promise a product the reaction could never deliver.

"The quiz is full of these," she said, and there was a small flatness in her voice, because she had gotten everything right except the thing that decided.

Anthony pushed his napkin toward her, then pulled it back, unsure whether showing was helping or whether she had to build her own road the way he had. Outside, a car door closed in the driveway. Tony looked at the window, then at the last slice of cheese.

"So do we split the extra cheese," he said, "or does it just sit there?"

"Split it," Anthony said, still watching the driveway.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: 'Bottom Line Up Front', or BLUF, is a US military writing standard that puts the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details.
story:
The co-op placement had seemed, on paper, like a chance to work with water. Wyatt had imagined himself at a river with a flow meter. Instead he sat at a desk at the regional conservation authority, three days a week, reading public comments about a proposal to expand a quarry and drafting replies he was never sure anyone wanted. His supervisor, Ms. Grant, spent most of her time in meetings, which left him alone with an inbox and the slow conviction that he was doing everything slightly wrong.

The problem arrived on a Tuesday. A hydrogeologist's report had flagged a possible risk to the aquifer beneath the quarry site, the same aquifer that supplied four hundred wells, and Ms. Grant had told him to summarize the public's concerns in an email to the ministry before Friday. Wyatt had written it that afternoon, all nine paragraphs, beginning with the history of the consultation process, moving through the composition of the volunteer committee, and arriving, somewhere near the sixth paragraph, at the point: the public wanted a second round of comment before any permit was issued. When he reread it, he could feel the request sinking under detail like a stone in still water.

He remembered, without meaning to, the year his father had drilled a well at the old house. The driller had been a phlegmatic man who answered every question with a pause and then one sentence, and when Wyatt's father had started explaining, at length, why he wanted the well placed near the garden, the man had held up a hand and said, "Tell me where you want the water first. Then tell me why." Wyatt had been twelve and had laughed about it for weeks. He was not laughing now.

At the break table the next morning, Knox was eating toast with the deliberate calm of someone who had done two years of this placement before him. Knox planned to monetize his GIS certificate eventually, consulting for developers, a plan Wyatt found vaguely distasteful and also enviable in its clarity. Wyatt showed him the email on his laptop.

"Nobody at the ministry reads past the first two lines," Knox said, crumbs on his sleeve. "My cousin's in the army reserve. They have a thing for this. Bottom Line Up Front, BLUF. Main point goes first, before any of the details."

"Sounds like a slogan."

"It works," Knox said. "Try it."

Wyatt tried it and disliked it immediately. The revision felt blunt, almost rude: three sentences stating the request, then the supporting material in descending order of importance, then an offer to provide the full submissions. All his careful context, the paragraphs he had built like an argument for his own seriousness, had to go or shrink. He kept both versions open on the screen and could not decide which one was honest. The long one represented how he actually thought, circling before committing. The short one represented what the reader needed, and he could not make those two things feel like the same virtue.

He was still deciding when Raya leaned over from the next desk, ostensibly to borrow a stapler. She read both versions in under a minute, which annoyed him. "The long one buries it," she said. "But don't cut the committee history entirely. That's the only part that shows this wasn't just you." She was right, he thought, and also her suggestion made the email longer again, and he sat for a while doing nothing with his hands on the keys.

He sent a hybrid before lunch: the request in the first three lines, the substance beneath it, one short paragraph on the consultation itself. Ms. Grant came back at four, read it standing beside his chair, and said only, "Good. They'll actually open this one." Whether that was praise for the structure or merely relief that the task was done, he couldn't tell, and he found he wanted to know, and then found he wanted to not be someone who needed to know.

That night he drafted a note to save in a folder called things I keep: that the way he'd always written, laying groundwork before the ask, was a habit from somewhere, maybe the well driller's yard, maybe earlier; that it might still be right for some readers and wrong for others; that Knox's rule and Raya's exception were both partly true and neither was his yet. He closed the laptop before he could make it tidier. Outside, the neighbour's sprinkler ticked across a dark lawn, spraying water no one would drink.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah lists 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle.
story:
Lea spread her notes across her grandmother's kitchen table while the kettle ticked on the stove. The debate assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Yang had drawn the topic out of a box without ceremony: does an ancient religious rule still bind people who live entirely modern lives. Lea had chosen the Sabbath, mostly because her grandmother kept it, and because keeping it meant her grandmother's television sat dark from Friday sundown to Saturday night, which Lea had never once thought to question until now.

Her phone buzzed. It was Alessandro, who had drawn the opposing side and seemed delighted about it.

"You know I'm going to destroy you," the message read. "Nobody under seventy believes you can't flip a light switch one day a week. My whole argument is that your side is aesthetic nostalgia."

Lea typed back with one hand while the other held her place in the book her grandmother had slid across the table that morning, a thick commentary with a cracked spine. "Then explain the 39 categories."

"That's not an argument, that's a trivia answer."

She set the phone face down and went back to the source. The Mishnah, her grandmother had said, list them out plainly. Lea had expected a scatter of prohibitions, but what she found was a structure: thirty-nine categories of work, and the rabbis linked them to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle. She read the line twice, then copied it onto her notecard in her smallest handwriting. Sowing, ploughing, baking, dyeing, spinning, kindling a fire, extinguishing a fire, carrying from one domain to another. Some of it was farming. Some of it was craft. None of it, on its face, was a phone.

Her grandmother came in with two glasses of juice and set one at Lea's elbow. She did not sit, which meant she intended to keep working, but she glanced at the notecard.

"So," Lea said. "Alessandro says the whole thing is nostalgia. He's going to stand up there and say nobody can tell him a phone is ploughing."

Her grandmother dried her hands on the towel very slowly. "What does the list say about electricity?"

"That's the thing. It doesn't say anything about electricity. It's about the Tabernacle. Wool and leather and fire." Lea turned the notecard over. "But carrying, that's on the list. Carrying from one domain to another. And I found this thing where people argue about whether completing a circuit is like building, or like kindling a fire, or neither. They impute the old category to the new thing. That's the whole fight, isn't it? Which old thing the new thing counts as."

Her grandmother took her glass and finally sat. "And what do you impute it to?"

"I don't know yet. That's the honest answer. Alessandro will say the rule is mercurial, that if it can stretch to cover whatever you want, it doesn't mean anything. And there's a version of him that's right. But there's another version where the stretching is the point. The rule was never about switches. It was about what counts as making something happen, and every generation has to ask that again with whatever it owns."

The kettle clicked off. Lea picked up the phone and typed a longer message than she meant to.

"Here's my actual position," she wrote. "The 39 categories come from the Mishnah, and the rabbis linked them to the work of building the Tabernacle. So the rule was always about a specific idea of creation, one day set against making. A phone isn't in the list because the list is a principle, not an inventory. When I pick it up on Saturday, I'm not violating a line about wool. I'm deciding whether an entire world in my pocket counts as the kind of domain they meant. I think it might. I'm not sure. But I'd rather argue from the text than from vibes, so bring your nostalgia speech and see how it goes."

Alessandro's reply took four minutes, long enough that Lea drank her juice and her grandmother went back to the counter.

"Fine," he wrote. "You get the text. I get common sense. Meet me Monday at lunch and we'll rehearse. Also your pragmatics are showing, you know that? Nobody says 'an inventory' out loud."

Lea laughed once, put the phone down, and pulled a fresh notecard toward her. At the top she wrote, in letters small enough to fit everything, "What stays uncertain." Below it she wrote a single question and underlined it twice.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
story:
The printer at his grandfather's house ran out of ink halfway through the assignment, so Tyson copied the graph onto tracing paper with a pencil, ruler and a hand that kept slipping. The sheet Ms. Rao had given them showed a sawtooth line climbing across sixty-some years, and underneath it three questions. The second one wanted the rise since the beginning, which meant he had to find the beginning first, and the smudged left edge gave him nothing.

"You're drawing," his grandfather said from the doorway, holding two mugs of tea he had apparently decided Tyson needed more than he did.

"Copying. It's for chemistry." Tyson set down the pencil. "Ms. Rao wants us to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read this graph, and present on Thursday. In front of everyone." He had volunteered for Thursday because Wednesday meant presenting before lunch, when nobody listened, and Friday meant the weekend would erase whatever he said. Thursday felt like a compromise between cowardice and ambition, though he could not have said so out loud.

His grandfather pulled a chair over and sat with his elbows on the table. He had spent thirty years reading rainfall charts for a water utility, and he looked at the tracing paper the way other people looked at photographs of their own children. "Start at the beginning," he said. "Not the beginning of your copying. The beginning of the data." He tapped the left edge with one dry finger. "Who measured this, and when?"

Tyson checked the small print he had squinted at on the bus, the sheet folded into quarters in his pocket. "Some observatory. Mauna Loa, in Hawaii. The first reading was March 1958." The pencil marks he had ruled showed the leftmost point sitting just above 310. "About three hundred thirteen parts per million," he said, and the number landed strangely in the room, so small and so heavy at once. Three hundred thirteen of what, though, was the question Meagan had texted him about that morning. Parts per million, he had written back. Like a pinch of salt in a swimming pool.

"There," his grandfather said. "Now you have an anchor. A surveyor never reads a map without knowing his first fixed point." He was quiet a moment, then added, "In my work we called the record a stratum, a layer of evidence laid down year by year. This line is the same thing. It won't lie to you, but it won't explain itself either."

That was the trouble. Tyson had the line, and he had the anchor, and between them stretched the whole rest of the problem, because Thursday required him to stand up and say why the line climbed, and he understood it only the way he understood photos in textbooks, as a thing that was true without being real to him. He took the second mug of tea mostly to have something in his hands.

He tried anyway, out loud, half to his grandfather and half to the tracing paper. Sunlight came through, he said, and the ground warmed up and wanted to give the heat back, and certain gases in the air let the light in but were slower to let the heat out, so a little extra stayed. Like a blanket, except a blanket you could not kick off. His grandfather nodded but did not rescue him, which Tyson had learned over many summers at this table was the old man's way of saying keep going.

"And the graph," Tyson went on. He put his fingertip at the left edge, at that first 1958 point. "It starts here, three thirteen. Every year after, a bit higher, higher, higher, and if I read off today's number and subtract, I get the rise." He did the subtraction twice on the back of a receipt and got the same answer both times, which almost never happened with his arithmetic. The sawtooth, he noticed, wasn't noise. It went down a little and up a little, down and up, riding on the climb. He thought of the seasons, Hawaii breathing in and breathing out, and though he could not prove it from the paper alone, he wrote it in the margin as a question for Ms. Rao rather than a claim.

Justina called at eight to argue about the presentation, because she thought they should open with the graph and Tyson thought they should open with the mechanism, the blanket idea, and get to the numbers second. "People's eyes glaze at numbers," she said. "People remember the blanket."

"People dismiss the blanket as a cartoon," Tyson said, "and then the graph is the proof. My grandfather says the record doesn't lie but it doesn't explain itself either." He looked over at the old man, who was pretending to read a crossword at the counter and visibly not reading it. "So maybe we do both. Blanket first, thirty seconds, then the line, then the anchor number, three thirteen in 1958, so everyone can see exactly how far it's moved since. Start where the data starts."

There was a pause on the line long enough that Tyson thought the call had dropped. "That's actually good," Justina said, in the grudging voice she saved for things she could not improve. "Say the part about the anchor exactly like that."

After she hung up, Tyson laid the tracing paper flat and worked through it once more, because Thursday was three days away and he was honest enough with himself to know that he understood the trapping part about seventy percent, well enough to explain it and not well enough to answer every question Ms. Rao might fire at him. He wrote that down too, in the margin, next to the question about the sawtooth: what I still can't explain. It felt penurious, that margin, a small and underfunded space for so much missing knowledge, but his grandfather had a saying about that too, something about how a surveyor's first fixed point was never the whole map, only the place you refused to guess from.

His grandfather came back to the table and set down the good lamp, the one with the adjustable neck, and angled it over the tracing paper until the pencil line stood out sharp and black. "Show me where it starts," he said. Tyson put his finger on the left edge, on 1958, on three hundred thirteen. The old man looked at it, then looked at him. "Now show me where it ends."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scores 180 countries and counts concentration of media ownership as one pressure on press freedom.
story:
I had done all my homework by Sunday evening, which was unusual enough that my mother kept touching my forehead. The essay was the problem, though. Mr. Fitzgerald had assigned a thousand words on "a story that matters to you and why," and I had picked the proposed data centre outside town, the one that would swallow two hundred acres of farmland if the rezoning passed. I had a stack of clippings. What I didn't have was a reason the coverage in the Herald had been so gentle, so fond of the word "progress," and why the Valley Examiner had called the same project a land grab in every single headline. I brought the clippings to dinner because our table is where things get settled, and also because I wanted an audience.

My father ate roast chicken and read the Herald's editorial at the same time, which he did most nights, folding the page into a quadrant so only his editorials showed. He said the data centre was a good thing and that I was too young to remember when this town had nothing. My mother said both sides had a point, which is what she says about everything, including cilantro. I laid out my clippings between the serving dishes and asked why two papers covering the same meeting had produced two different planets.

"Ownership," my father said, with the satisfaction of a man laying down a trump card. "The Examiner's owned by that family that's been feuding with the county for thirty years. Of course it's scathing. It's practically a newsletter."

He said it like that settled everything. It settled nothing for me, because if the Herald's owner also had interests, and I was fairly sure it did, then both papers were newsletters and I had no way of knowing which planet was real. I said this. My father said that was cynicism, and cynicism, he said, was lazy. I pointed out that he was the one who had dismissed an entire newspaper over a feud. My mother refilled the water glasses.

Here is where I should be honest, since nobody else at that table was going to be. I told them I'd read an international index that proved ownership was a measurable pressure on press freedom, and I said it in a voice like I'd known it for years. I had not read it. I had seen Malorie mention something in a group chat two days earlier and hadn't opened the link. Malorie is the person who reads footnotes for fun, and I'd been meaning to ask her. At the time I presented it as settled scholarship, which is a habit of mine that my father calls pedantry and that I call winning. The problem with being an unreliable narrator of your own dinner is that everyone can fact-check you in real time, and I was sitting next to the good wifi.

She was already typing when I texted. "RSF. Reporters Without Borders. They publish the World Press Freedom Index. It's been published since 2002. It scores 180 countries."

"And ownership?" I typed, one-handed under the table, which my mother pretended not to notice with such commitment that she watched the ceiling.

"It counts concentration of media ownership as one of the pressures on press freedom. It's literally part of the score."

I looked up our country's rank while my father explained to the chicken that inheritance tax was theft. The number was higher than I'd guessed, not a disaster, not a triumph, and the site's write-up treated ownership concentration the way it treated jailed journalists and lawsuits, as one pressure among several, a thing you could weigh rather than a thing that proved all news was a lie. That distinction mattered to me more than I expected. My father's version of the ownership argument was a wrecking ball. The index used it more like a level, something you set on the table to see how crooked the table was.

I read the rank out loud. My father said he didn't believe anything with the word "borderless" in it.
