I said it was "Without Borders," not "Borderless," and that this particular pedantry was, for once, load-bearing, and that our country ranked exactly where it ranked whether he believed it or not. He asked who funded the index. I said I didn't know yet, and that this was a fair question, which surprised him more than the argument had. My mother said the potatoes were getting cold, and they were, and we ate them cold, which in our house counts as a concession on all sides.

Kaitlyn went upstairs after dinner and opened the essay document. It still said nothing but the title and her name, which it had said for four days, whatever she'd told her mother about having finished her homework. She wrote half a paragraph about the two planets, then deleted "planets" because it sounded like she was showing off, then put it back. She had the fact now, the real one, with its date and its number of countries and its plain treatment of ownership as one pressure among others, and she had two ways of using it. One was the wrecking ball, her father's way, which felt satisfying and let her stop thinking. The other was the level, which obliged her to keep reading, to find out who owned both papers, to weigh the feud against the fondness for the word "progress," and she could not yet say where that would end.

She texted Malorie to say thank you and also that Malorie was insufferable in the specific way that had saved her essay. Malorie sent back a single question mark, which was fair. Below Kaitlyn's window her father was walking the dog along the fence line in the dark, the Herald folded in his jacket pocket, and from this angle she couldn't tell whether he was reading it or just carrying it.

She typed: "The Herald's owner turns out to sit on the county's economic development board."

Then she sat with that sentence for a while, cursor blinking, and finally moved it down two paragraphs, because she wasn't sure yet what it underpinned and what it merely decorated. "I'm eating the last of the chicken," she called down the stairs, and she did.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The truck's passenger seat had a crack running across it, and Nicole kept her thumb pressed into it while her dad drove. Behind them, in the mirrored trailer, sat twenty-two boxes and her mattress on its side. She had taped one box herself, the night before, with her name on it in marker so the movers would not lose track of whose it was, as if any of it could be anyone else's.

Her phone buzzed against her thigh at the second rest stop. Kael had sent a photo of the school parking lot, empty on a Saturday, with the caption "50 hours left to go." She understood the joke immediately. On their last lunch together, Elisha had read something off her phone and announced that a researcher named Jeffrey Hall had done a study in 2018 estimating it took roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Kael had said that explained why Marcus, from chemistry, still felt like a stranger after a semester of lab partners. Nicole had laughed, and then had not laughed, because a number like that was not funny to someone with a moving truck idling outside her house.

She typed "46 to go" and sent it back, and then sat on the concrete barrier beside the vending machines while her dad bought coffee. Fifty hours. She tried to convert it into something she could hold: two full days of being awake, or five school weeks of lunch periods, or an entire season of sitting next to someone in class and hoping. The arithmetic was not hard. What was hard was deciding whether the number augured well or badly, whether it meant friendship was achievable through sheer attendance or that it was slow and mechanical, a meter filling up at a fixed rate regardless of what she did.

The truck cab smelled like her dad's coffee and the cardboard that had warmed in the sun all morning. At a red light outside some town with three water towers, he asked whether she wanted to pick the radio station, and she said sure, and turned it to the one Kael always played in his car, and the signal dissolved into static forty minutes later. That was happenstance, she supposed, the station's range ending exactly where her old life did, but it felt staged, like the world showing off.

They stopped at a motel with a pool that had been drained. Her dad took the room key and she took the ice bucket down the hall for no reason, just to have a task. She called Elisha from the laundry room, sitting on a dryer that someone had left running.

"How many hours do we have," Elisha said, instead of hello.

"I don't know. I never counted ours."

"That's the point, though. Nobody counts the ones that work." There was a pause, and the dryer thumped under Nicole's legs. "Hall only gives you the first number. Casual friend at fifty. He doesn't say how long the real ones take, or whether distance runs the clock backward."

Nicole had not thought of that, that the study might run in reverse, that hours apart could subtract. "So it's capricious," she said. "Not the study. The thing itself."

"Or the study is honest and the thing is. I can't tell from here."

They stayed on the phone for an hour and eleven minutes, which Nicole only noticed when she hung up, and she did the subtraction before she could stop herself and decided she would not tell Elisha the total. Some accounting you kept private.

The new house had a driveway wide enough for the truck to back in without clipping the mailbox. Nicole carried her named box up the stairs first, set it on the bare floor of the room with the window facing east, and opened it. Inside were the things she had packed in the last hour before bed: her debate trophies, a shoebox of notes passed in class, the cheap camera, and the folded map of her old town that Elisha had drawn from memory as a going-away present, with an X on the diner and an X on the spot by the river where they had all once gotten stuck in the mud.

Her dad called up that the movers wanted to know where the mattress went. She stood at the window a moment longer. School started in three weeks, and she understood now that she could hold both ideas at once: that fifty hours was a real number, a floor under her feet, something to rely on; and that no number covered Elisha's map or Kael's photo, which had either defied the math or existed outside it. She could not resolve that and she was not going to pretend to.

"Second room on the left," she called down the stairs, and went to help carry it in.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
story:
The worksheet had traveled three hundred miles folded into the side pocket of Julia's backpack, and now it sat between two marshmallow sticks on the picnic table, one corner damp from the morning dew. Mr. Shapiro, who taught geography and had agreed to run this trip only after the principal promised it would be small, had assigned it before they left: pick a country, read its population pyramid, and write a paragraph predicting whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes. Julia had chosen Japan mostly because Elle had already claimed Brazil, and Maverick, sprawled across the fire log with his hat over his face, had said he would take Nigeria and then apparently taken nothing at all, including the assignment, seriously.

"You're doing homework at a lake," Maverick said, lifting the brim of his hat an inch.

"I'm doing homework at a table beside a lake," Julia said. "Those are different things." She turned the worksheet toward the gray light. The pyramid looked like a fir tree upside down, wide at the bottom, narrowing fast, and near the top it did something she had not expected. The two sides were not symmetrical. The left side of each band fell away while the right side stayed thick, so that among the oldest cohorts the shape leaned, subtly but everywhere, in one direction.

Elle came over with a mug of oatmeal and looked at the page upside down. "Why is yours lopsided?"

"That's what I'm trying to figure out." Julia ran her pencil along the eighty-five-plus bar. Left side, thin. Right side, noticeably wider. She checked seventy to seventy-four. The same lean. She checked a printed pyramid for France in the textbook Mr. Shapiro had brought for kindling and refused to burn, and the lean was there too, at the very top, like a flag bent by a wind nobody had drawn.

Maverick rolled off the log and put his chin on the table. "My guess is the government lies about the men," he said. "Or the men all, like, emigrate to Portugal."

"That's gratuitous," Elle said. "There's a simpler answer and you know it."

"There is?" Julia said.

Elle stirred her oatmeal and looked, for a moment, like she was deciding whether to say it. She was the person in their class who kept a mental list of facts the way other people kept stickers on a laptop, and she had learned the hard way, in seventh grade, that correcting people could cost you a lunch table. Julia remembered watching her swallow a correction about the Nile once, and watching the boy repeat his wrong version to the whole room. Elle had never mentioned it. Julia had never asked why she stayed quiet, and she thought about that now, how a person could be right and choose silence, and whether that was generosity or just defeat wearing a nicer coat.

"The top of most population pyramids has more women than men," Elle said finally, "because women live longer than men on average." She pointed at the right-hand side of Julia's pyramid. "That's the female side. That's why it's wider up there."

Julia looked at the shape again and felt it rearrange itself in her mind, the way a chemistry problem did when you finally saw that the monomer was the whole point of the polymer. "So when I'm deciding about nursing homes," she said slowly, "I'm mostly deciding about places for women. That changes the paragraph."

"It should change the paragraph," Maverick said. "That's what makes it interesting. Otherwise you're just counting rectangles."

Mr. Shapiro came down from the fire with the coffee pot and stood at the end of the table, saying nothing, which was his way of teaching. Julia laid the pencil down. She had wanted the assignment to be arithmetic, bars in, answer out, and now it was something with a lean in it. She could predict that Japan would need more nursing homes before it needed more schools; the narrow base made that clear enough. But the prediction had a texture she had not planned for, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she did not know what to do with it yet. She thought of her grandmother, who lived alone and called every Sunday, and of the way her mother always ended the call early.

She wrote one line at the bottom of the worksheet, then crossed it out and wrote another. Elle watched over her shoulder and said, "You're going to problematize a prediction about rectangles?"

"I'm going to be accurate," Julia said. "The right side is wider at the top. The nursing homes will be fuller of grandmothers than grandfathers, and I think a prediction that leaves that out is a worse prediction."

Maverick put his hat back over his face. "It's a paragraph, not a treaty."

"It's practice," Julia said, and folded the worksheet along its old crease.

They hiked out that afternoon along the ridge trail, and at the overlook Mr. Shapiro let them stop for ten minutes. Julia stood at the rail with her backpack straps in both hands. Below, the valley held a town with a school at one end and, near the church, a long low building she recognized by its shape without being able to say how she recognized it. Elle came to stand beside her.

"Still thinking about old women?" Elle asked.

"Still thinking about whether I said thank you," Julia said.

Elle bumped her shoulder against Julia's shoulder and turned back toward the trail, and Julia followed her down, the worksheet riding dry against her back.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: The Surrealist André Breton described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb," though Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label.
story:
The art room smelled of turpentine and the lemon disinfectant the janitor used on Fridays, and Seth sat with his critique essay flat on the table in front of him like something that had died there. On the wall, Mr. Rahimi had projected a reproduction of Kahlo's The Two Fridas, two women seated hand in hand on a bench, one in white European dress, one in Tehuana dress, a vein running between their exposed hearts.

"You're reading it like a book report," Jai said, leaning across the table. "She painted this, she painted that. Mr. Rahimi wants formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Not feelings about feelings."

"I know what he wants. I just don't know how to want it." Seth tapped his pen against the paper, where he had written, and crossed out, and rewritten, the same opening sentence three times. The thing was, when he looked at the painting, he did feel something, a pressure behind his sternum like the vein in the picture had been threaded through him too. Turning that into a paragraph about composition felt like dissecting something that had been alive an hour ago.

Jai spun the printout toward himself. "Okay, start with the symmetry. Two figures, mirror halves, but the colours fight. White lace against the deep red of the heart, the stormy sky behind. The composition is balanced and it's bleeding. That's your thesis." He said it with the easy authority of someone who had already finished his own essay, and probably had footnotes.

Seth remembered then the afternoon last spring when he had tried to teach himself to draw faces, sitting at the kitchen table with a library book open to Kahlo's self-portraits while his mother made tea and his little brother kept grabbing the pencils. He had spent two hours on her eyebrows alone, the meeting of them like a bird in flight, and had finally understood, in a small and bodily way, that every strange choice in her face was deliberate. Nothing was accidental. Even the hair on her upper lip, painted frankly, without apology. He had been fourteen and it had been the first time art made him feel addressed, spoken to directly.

"Cruz called her a Surrealist in his critique," Jai said now, lowering his voice although Cruz was across the room arguing with someone about whether glitter counted as a medium. "Mr. Rahimi wrote 'check this' in the margin. It was beautiful. Cruz was so smug about it, too."

Seth frowned. "Is she? The double self, the exposed heart, that's dreamlike, isn't it?"

"Look it up before you put it in your essay. That's all I'm saying. You don't want a truculent margin note on your paper like Cruz got."

Seth pulled out his phone, typing carefully, and found it quickly: the Surrealist André Breton had described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb." He read the line twice. It was a gorgeous phrase, and it flattered the paintings, and then, further down the page, he found the second part. Kahlo herself had later rejected the Surrealist label. She had said, in effect, that she painted her own reality, not her dreams.

"Wait," Seth said, out loud, before he could shape it into anything. "She said no."

"Who said no to what?"

"Kahlo. Breton called her work a ribbon around a bomb, called her a Surrealist, and she rejected the label. She didn't want to be filed under his movement." Seth sat with that a moment, the phone warm in his hand. The painting on the wall looked different now, or he looked at it differently, which amounted to the same thing. He had been treating the strange elements, the joined vein, the scissors, the storm, as if they came from somewhere outside her, a dreamland she'd wandered into. But if she painted her own reality, then the strangeness was the reality. The doubled self wasn't fantasy. It was a diary in a language that ordinary words couldn't reach.

"So which is she?" Jai asked. "Is the critique Surrealist or not?"

"I don't think that's the right question." Seth pulled his essay back and began writing in the margin, fast, his handwriting deteriorating with speed. "Breton saw a ribbon. She was the bomb. He looked at her pain and saw decoration, or style, and she was saying, no, this is a record. This happened to my body, to my country, to my two heritages pulled apart on one bench." He paused. "But I can't prove what he meant by it. Maybe he meant it as praise. I have to be honest that I'm reading his ribbon and her rejection and making something of it that neither of them exactly said."

Jai made a face. "Mr. Rahimi loves that kind of hedging, though. He calls it intellectual honesty. The rest of us call it covering your grade."

Mr. Rahimi drifted past their table on his rounds, a coffee cup in one hand, and glanced at Seth's margin scrawl without stopping. "Better," he said, which from him was a paragraph.

Seth recalibrate

Seth recalibrated his opening sentence for the fourth time, and this time it held. Colour: the surgical white against arterial red. Composition: the symmetry that refuses to comfort. Symbolism: a vein that connects two selves, and a pair of scissors held in a lap like an instrument and a threat. He wrote until the bell, and then a little past the bell, while Jai packed his bag and Cruz, still truculent about glitter, slammed his portfolio shut.

Outside the window the afternoon had gone the grey of Kahlo's storm sky, coincidentally, and Seth copied his last line into his notebook before the projection was switched off: She gave him a ribbon; she kept the bomb.

"Coming?" Jai said from the doorway.

"In a minute." Seth looked once more at the blank screen where the two Fridas had been, then capped his pen and followed him out.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel The Good Soldier opens with its narrator, John Dowell, saying, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.'
story:
Lily spread the paperback on the kitchen table between a bowl of cereal going soft and her mother's unopened bank statements, and read the first line again. "This is the saddest story I have ever heard." She had read it four times since Sunday, and each time it bothered her a little more, the way a word repeated too often starts to look misspelled. The novel was Ford Madox Ford's The Good Soldier, published in 1915, and Ms. Whitehead had assigned it with the warning that the narrator, John Dowell, could not exactly be trusted. Lily had assumed that meant he lied. Now she suspected it was something stranger.

She texted Ekam, who had finished the book in two days and claimed to have understood it entirely. "why does dowell say heard," she typed. "he was there. it's his own life."

Ekam's reply came in bursts. "right?? that's the whole thing." Then, "he tells it like someone told it to him. like he wasn't even in the room when his own marriage happened." Then a picture of his cat asleep on his copy of the book, spine cracked flat, which was Ekam's way of saying he was done thinking about it for the night.

Lily's mother came through in her work clothes, put a hand on the kettle, and glanced at the table. "Is that for school? Good, school. Better than that phone." She said things like this now, in a bright, effortful voice, ever since Lily's father had moved his things to the apartment across town in March. Lily had learned to answer the voice rather than the words underneath it.

"English," Lily said. "It's about a man who narrates his own life like it's a rumor."

Her mother laughed, a real one, surprising them both. "I know people like that." She carried her tea toward the hallway, then stopped. "Your dad called. He wants to take you dinner Friday, that place you liked." The kettle ticked as it cooled. Lily turned a page she wasn't reading.

"Italian place," she said. "The one with the terrible paintings."

"The very one." Her mother's voice went bright again, and she left before either of them could decide what the invitation meant.

Lily marked the page and tried to work it out on paper, because Ms. Whitehead kept saying an essay was just thinking that had slowed down enough to be inspected. If Dowell says heard, she wrote, then either he is not perspicacious enough to notice the gap, or he notices it and cannot bear to own the story, so he hands it off, makes himself a listener. She stared at that. Both could be true at once. That was the part that kept snagging: a narrator could be deceived and self-deceiving in the same paragraph, and the reader had to hold both without letting either one absolve him. She thought of her mother's bright voice, and of her father's letters, which were warm and vague and arranged events so that no one had ever decided anything. Everyone in her house was narrating lately, and every version was sincere, which made it worse.

The next afternoon Erin came over to work on the presentation they were splitting, and they read the opening aloud in the living room, trading sentences, doing the voices. Erin gave Dowell a pompous BBC accent that made Lily laugh so hard she had to put the book down. "He's like a man giving a eulogy at his own funeral," Erin said, "and congratulating himself on how moved he is."

"But that's the argument," Lily said, sitting up. "He calls it a story he heard. He heard it. His own marriage, and he says heard. So the question for the essay is whether the reader trusts him less or more because of it, and I keep flip flopping."

"Then flip flop in the essay," Erin said. "Ms. Whitehead loves that. Write both sides and admit which one you can't decide."

"I can't decide because the evidence is him. The evidence is the problem." Lily flopped back against the couch cushions. "If I wrote my life like that, third person, saddest story I ever heard, you'd think I was either lying or dying."

"You'd do the Italian place voice," Erin said. "Devastating."

Later, after Erin left, Lily sat at the kitchen table with the laptop open and her half of the presentation saved, and wrote the first sentence of the essay draft: "John Dowell calls The Good Soldier the saddest story he has ever heard, though it is the story of his own life, and that single verb, heard, is where the reader's trust begins to wobble." She read it over. It was a claim, not a conclusion, which she told herself was honest rather than lazy. Her phone buzzed: her father, confirming Friday, seven o'clock, and asking, in the way he asked things, whether she wanted the corner table by the bad painting of the vineyard. She typed yes, then deleted it, then typed it again and sent it, and turned back to the screen, where the cursor sat blinking after the word wobble. "He heard it," she said to the empty kitchen, and started the second sentence.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and burnt insulation, and the pit tables ran in rows under fluorescent lights all the way to the bleachers. Stella set her laptop on the folding table between the toolbox and the spare battery, opened her code, and found the bug still sitting where she had left it at two in the morning. The robot, a squat drivetrain with an arm that was supposed to lift a cone, refused to report its arm position to the dashboard. Everything else worked. It was as if the arm did not know it existed.

She had written a class called Arm to hold the arm's state. It had private fields, position and target, and getter methods to read them. That was the new thing, the thing Mr. Oliveira had assigned the week before the competition: stop keeping everything in one bloated file, learn to build a class properly, then test it. She had tested it, she thought. The tests passed. And yet when the robot ran, the dashboard showed zeros, always zeros, like a river gauge above a dried-up riparian channel, reporting nothing while the water was gone.

Dana leaned over her shoulder with a bag of pretzels. "Still zeros?"

"Still zeros." Stella scrolled through the class. "The getters are right. The fields are private, like they're supposed to be. I initialize everything."

Jaylen arrived with the scouting clipboard and the expression of someone who had opinions about the third match. He looked at the screen for four seconds and pointed at a line. "Why does your constructor say void?"

Stella looked. Her constructor, the method meant to run when the Arm object was created, was written public void Arm, with the fields set inside it. "Because it's a method," she said. "Methods get return types. That's the rule."

"Is it, though," Jaylen said, and ate one of Dana's pretzels without asking.

The announcer called teams to queue for practice matches, and Stella put the laptop to sleep and carried the robot to the field, where their alliance partner dropped a cone in a way that suggested the cone had wronged them personally. Stella drove. She drove well, actually, better than in the last competition, threading the narrow gap behind the junction post. But the whole time she was turning the joystick she was thinking about the word void, about how she had put it there without thinking, the way you add a seatbelt to a car that didn't need one.

Back at the pit, she opened the class again and did what she had been refusing to do since two in the morning: she read her own code as if a stranger had written it. She deleted the word void in front of Arm and nothing else. Then she wrote a test. She created a new Arm object and immediately called the getters, expecting the values she had set. Before the change, the getters had returned zeros, because the constructor never ran at all. After the change, the test printed the values she expected, and she sat back and said, out loud, "It's not a void method. A constructor has no return type. It just has the same name as the class and nothing in front of it."

"So it's not even a method," Dana said.

"I don't know what it is. I know what it isn't." Stella wrote the fact in the margin of her notebook, in pen, next to a drawing of a fish she could not explain later.

Mr. Oliveira came by during the lunch break with a cup of coffee and asked how the refactor was going. Stella showed him the before and after, the single deleted word. He nodded once. "Half of debugging is finding out which of your rules was never a rule."

She had assumed it was a rule because it looked like one. Every method she had ever written had a return type, so her hand had transliterated the pattern onto something that looked like a method but obeyed a different grammar. It had felt like rigor. Now she suspected it had been closer to an affectation, a formal gesture applied where it didn't belong, like wearing a lab coat to fix a toaster. She thought about her father, who believed in following instructions exactly, and her coach, who believed in breaking things until they confessed. She had spent a year trying to decide which of them was right, and here was a third option: rules were local. You had to find out where each one stopped.

Between matches, Jaylen asked whether she wanted him to look over the rest of the code for missing return types. She had been ready earlier to hand him the laptop and let him be the one who knew. "No," she said. "I'll read it myself. But stay close in case I start adding semicolons to my breakfast."

Qualification matches ran late. The arm worked all afternoon, the dashboard reporting real numbers, and Stella kept glancing at them the way you glance at a door you finally locked. They were ranked eleventh when alliance selection began, and when the second-seeded captain read the names off the card, theirs was not among them. Dana started packing the toolbox. Jaylen stood with the clipboard against his chest, watching the field.

Stella closed her laptop halfway, then opened it again and started a new file. "Next year's class," she said. "I'm writing the constructor first this time."

"Without the void?"

"Without the void," she said, and typed the class name twice, once for the file and once for the line that would run.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
Jake turned eighteen on the fourth of October, and the election was on the seventh, which meant that for three days he carried around the small private weight of being someone whose opinion now counted. He had registered in September at the library, printing his name in block letters while a woman with a lanyard watched, and the card had come in the mail last week, addressed to Mr. Jacob Reyes, which nobody had ever called him. He kept it in the back pocket of his jeans like a license he hadn't tested yet.

On the sixth he walked to the coffee shop on Mercer Street after his last class, because Janie had texted him that she and Carley were collating the voter guides there, stapling pages for the renters' association, and because he wanted, without being able to say so, to be near people who had already decided. The shop smelled of burnt espresso and wet cardboard. Mr. Papadopoulos was behind the counter, wiping down the machine with the slow, glacial patience of a man who had closed ten thousand times before and would close ten thousand times again.

"He's going to be a first-timer," Janie announced when Jake sat down. "Look at him. He has the face of someone about to choose a college, except it's the whole country."

"Two candidates," Carley said, not looking up from the stapler. "Statistically easier than colleges." She was working through a stack of guides with the efficiency of someone who had done this for her mother's union before, squaring the pages, driving the staple through the corner, setting the finished guide on a rising pile.

Jake bought a hot chocolate he didn't want so he could justify the table. "It's not the choosing," he said. "It's that everyone else seems to know."

Mr. Papadopoulos drifted over with a rag and began clearing the neighboring table, though it was already clear. "In my country you voted because everyone voted," he said. "Here it is a kind of religion. You choose to come to the church." He laughed at his own joke and went back to the counter, and Jake thought about that longer than the joke probably deserved.

Carley snapped a staple free of a jam. "It's weirder than that. I was doing a comparison for Mr. Papadopoulos's civics thing last night, country by country. Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and if you don't vote without a valid reason you can be fined." She looked up, waiting.

"Paid," Jake said. "People actually pay it?"

"Apparently, or they show up. It's just normal there." She drove the staple home. "Meanwhile here my uncle has skipped three presidential elections because, quote, it stresses him out."

Janie turned a guide over in her hands. "So in one place it's a duty they make you do, and in ours it's a freedom most people leave on the shelf." She said it lightly, but Jake felt the floor of the conversation tilt, because he had been sitting on something for two weeks, and it had begun to feel like the thing the whole election was actually about.

His father had been laid off from the plant in June. The incumbent's party had taken credit for saving the plant in a speech that got played on the news, and his father had watched it from the couch and said nothing, and his mother had said nothing, and the silence had settled over the house like weather. His father's friends, the ones from the union hall, were all voting the same direction, loudly, and Jake had assumed for most of the autumn that he would vote that direction too. It was almost automatic. Then the challenger had come to the high school gymnasium in September and said a thing about the river that Jake couldn't stop turning over, a specific promise about the dredging permits, and Jake had looked it up, and it checked out, and he had told no one.

His phone buzzed against the table. A message from his father, the first of the week: "Big day tomorrow. First one. Whatever you do, do it like it counts, because it does. Proud of you either way." Jake read it twice under the table, thumb shading the screen. He did not show it to Janie or Carley. He noticed that his father hadn't said who to vote for, which meant either that his father trusted him, or that his father assumed there was no question, and Jake could not tell which, and the not-telling felt like its own small betrayal on someone's part, though he couldn't say whose.

"What?" Janie said. "You went somewhere."

"Nothing. My dad." He put the phone face down. Outside, the streetlights were coming on along Mercer, one and then the next, a slow relay. Carley kept stapling. Mr. Papadopoulos turned the sign on the door, and in the window's reflection Jake could see himself sitting between his two friends, small and doubled, holding a cooling hot chocolate with both hands.

"You know what I think," Janie said, leaning in. "Nobody knows. They just stop admitting it."

"I think I know one thing," Jake said. "I think the fine is not the reason anybody should vote, and neither is anybody's couch." Carley raised her eyebrows at that, and he felt himself flush, because it had come out sharper than he meant, closer to home than he had planned to go.

They walked out together at closing, and at the corner where the three of them split, Janie said, "So? Tomorrow?" Jake said, "Tomorrow," and put his hands in his pockets, and the voter card was there, soft at the corners already from carrying, and he walked the long way home past the gymnasium so he could look at it in the dark.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The banner had come out wrong, and there was no time to fix it. Someone, and Violet strongly suspected Gage, had written CONGRATULATIONS LADIES VOLLEYBALL on the long strip of paper taped above the bleachers, except the season was basketball, and the "L" in VOLLEYBALL drooped like a fainting swan. Violet stood in the gym with the trophy box under one arm and considered her options, which were: take it down and have nothing, leave it up and be wrong forever, or find a third thing.

"We could cut it into a scarf," Inaya said, appearing beside her with a bag of chips already open. "It's cold in here. That could presage a long winter."

"That's not what presage means for scarves," Violet said, though honestly she wasn't sure what it meant for scarves either. She dragged the folding table to center court while the seniors trickled in from the locker room, damp-haired, moving slowly the way people move when they know a thing is ending and would rather not arrive at the end too quickly.

Mr. Mehta, who coached them and also taught psychology third period, came in carrying the folding chairs himself, refusing help on principle. "Nobody sits on the floor on my watch," he announced, which was a lie, because they sat on the floor constantly, but it was his particular idiosyncrasy, along with the whistle he wore to parties.

The problem of the banner solved itself in the worst way. Gage, arriving late with the cake, stopped dead under it and read it out loud, twice, with increasing delight. "Ladies volleyball. Ladies. Volleyball." The seniors groaned. Someone threw a rolled-up sock at him. Violet felt the party tilting toward an hour of teasing and away from anything that mattered, and she had been planning, secretly, for it to matter.

Here was her real problem, worse than the banner: this was the last time all nine of them would be in one room as a team. Four seniors were graduating, two were moving, and next year's tryouts would assemble a different animal entirely. She had wanted to say something about that, something true, and she had nothing but a half-remembered line from Mr. Mehta's class that she might be getting wrong.

She climbed onto the folding table anyway, holding the trophy box like a pulpit. "Okay, listen. One announcement."

"You're announcing the volleyball team," Gage said.

"Shut up, Gage." But she was smiling, and she let the laugh happen, because the laugh made the room warm, and warm rooms hold words better. "So. In psych, Mr. Mehta told us about Tuckman. The group stages guy. Forming, storming, norming, performing. But in 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate." She paused. The word sat in the gym like a basketball nobody wanted to pick up. "That's us. Tonight. We're adjourning."

"That's the saddest announcement I've ever heard," Inaya said, but she said it quietly, and she came and stood closer to the table.

"I thought about making a sign," Violet went on, "like a stage sign, adjourning, with an arrow. And I couldn't decide if that's honoring it or ruining it. Like, is naming the thing the same as feeling it? I genuinely don't know." She found she was talking faster, the honest kind of fast. "Maybe it's like the banner. It's wrong, and we keep it anyway, because it's ours and it's wrong."

There was a silence with cake in its future. Then one of the seniors, the tall one who never spoke in huddles, said, "We storming at any point? Because Tuesday practice, when Gage and Coach argued about the zone defense for forty minutes, that felt like storming."

"That was norming," Gage said. "We normed so hard."

"It was a hurricane of norming," Violet agreed, and the room broke open laughing, and she climbed down off the table having said the thing and not knowing if she'd said it well, which she decided was the only honest way to say anything.

They ate cake on the floor. Mr. Mehta pretended not to see. Gage got the piece with the drooping frosting, which everyone agreed served him right, and when someone suggested he was now "cake-indigent," he defended himself so seriously, with such citations of frosting law, that Inaya had to lie flat on the court to recover.

Near the end, when the seniors were taking down the net for the last time, Violet climbed the bleachers and took the banner down herself. She folded it, VOLLEYBALL inward, and gave it to the tall senior. "Evidence," she said. "That we happened." The senior held it against her chest with both arms, like a rebound in the final second, and walked out through the double doors into the parking lot lights.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale.
story:
The party was in Kaelan's backyard, string lights sagging between the fence and the garage, and Brandon arrived holding a bag of ice nobody had asked him to bring. He set it in the cooler beside the sodas and stayed near the drinks table for a while, which everyone understood to mean he was not ready to be anywhere else. Nahla pulled him toward the lawn chairs eventually, and the three of them sat in the smell of citronella while someone's playlist argued quietly with a mosquito zapper.

"You're not leaving until Saturday," Kaelan said, as though correcting an error in a paper.

"Friday night, actually. The truck comes Friday morning." Brandon peeled the label off his bottle in one long strip. He had planned to say something rehearsed, something about visiting at Thanksgiving, but when the moment came he heard himself say, "I keep thinking I'll be fine, and then I think maybe I won't, and I can't tell which of those thoughts is the honest one."

Nahla, who had spent the summer at her sister's apartment near the university, tilted her head. "My sister was a wreck her first month. She had this whole theory she was uniquely broken by it. Then her roommate cried over a shower curtain, of all things, because it looked like the one at home."

"That's supposed to comfort me?"

"I looked it up, actually. Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale. So a fifth of them have it bad enough to measure halfway up the scale or higher. She made me memorize it like a spell."

Brandon turned the fact over. Nearly everyone, which meant it wasn't a defect; a fifth above the midpoint, which meant most people sat below it, missing things and still functioning. He tried to prognosticate from these numbers, to calculate his own future from a sample he'd never met, and understood at once that this was impossible, that the statistics described a population and not a person, and that he would find out which fifth he belonged to only by going. "So there's a four in five chance I'm only moderately miserable," he said.

"That is the most Brandon way to hear good news," Kaelan said, laughing. "You've turned it into odds."

Earlier that week, Brandon's father had called homesickness "a kind of parasitism of the mind," a phrase he'd picked up from some podcast, suggesting the feeling lived off you and gave nothing back. Brandon had nodded at the time, but now, sitting with the actual numbers, the idea seemed specious, glib, a neat sound pretending to be a truth. Missing people who mattered didn't drain him; it was evidence of the thing itself, the friendships, the house, the street with the crooked stop sign. He didn't say any of this aloud. He just thought: the feeling is the receipt, not the debt.

Ms. Ba came out from the kitchen with a tray of spring rolls her mother had sent for the occasion, and she pressed one into Brandon's hand before he could refuse. "You will write to me in English, yes? And not only when you need a recommendation letter." He promised, and she looked at him a moment longer than necessary, the way she had in class when she knew an essay was better than the student believed it was, and then she went back inside.

Kaelan brought out an old badminton set with only one intact racket and a shuttlecock the dog had chewed, and they played a lopsided game in the dark, Nahla keeping score with numbers she invented freely, Brandon lunging and laughing and losing badly on purpose and then, on one point, genuinely trying, his whole body reaching for the bird as it drifted over the string-lit fence and into the neighbor's tomato plants. He climbed over, retrieved it, and stood for a second on the far side looking back at the lit yard, at the two of them waving him home. Then he dropped the shuttlecock over the fence first, and climbed back to catch it before it hit the grass.
